Chapter 3 Constitutive equations

3.1 The tension test

How strongly a material resists stretching cannot be computed from equilibrium. We have to measure it. The simplest test is the one we have been doing in thought since the beginning of the book: we pull a bar along its axis and measure the force and the elongation. It is called the tension test (natezni preizkus). The goal of this section is to get from the tension test the relation between stress and strain for a given material, to write it with two numbers, and to use it to answer two questions we left open: why in section 2.2 the quotient of the stress in the hanging bar and the number 196 GPa gave its strain, and what its displacement \(u(x)\) is.

Why a bar? Because in its middle part the stress and the strain are almost the same at all points. In a bar pulled by a force \(F\) at both ends, the axial force in every cross section is \(N = F\) (section 2.1). Far from the ends this force is spread almost evenly over the cross section (section 2.2). If the material is the same along the whole bar, all pieces between marks on the bar therefore get longer by the same amount (the middle bar in figure 1.25). So we get the stress \(N/A\) and the strain \(\Delta L/L\) from one measured force and one measured elongation, and both hold at every point between the two marks. Where the stress and the strain change from point to point, one force and one elongation do not tell us which stress belongs to which strain. The right bar in the same figure shows this, hanging under its own weight: the top piece is stretched the most, the bottom one hardly at all, and yet the total elongation is the same as for the middle bar. From the total elongation we get only the average \(\Delta L/L\), which does not tell how a single piece is stretched. It would be the same for a body of a more complicated shape. This is why we measure the relation between stress and strain on a specimen in which both are uniform (BOWER, PDF p. 93).

From history

Hooke, Mariotte and Coulomb, whom we met in section 1.1, did their experiments mainly to check a particular theory. In the eighteenth century, however, builders needed data on the strength of the materials they used (TIMO, PDF p. 62). Petrus van Musschenbroek, professor of physics at Utrecht and later at Leiden, therefore carried out an extensive series of tests and described them in a work of 1729 (TIMO, PDF p. 62-63).

Musschenbroek's machine pulled the bar through levers that magnified the force (TIMO, PDF p. 63). How a lever magnifies a force is shown by the scheme on the left of figure 3.3. The lever is a rigid rod that can turn about a support. On the long arm \(a\) hangs a weight \(G\), and on the short arm \(c\) on the other side of the support the bar is attached, which is fixed to the ground below and which the lever pulls upward. The lever is at rest when the moments of the two forces about the support are equal, so the bar is pulled by the force \(G\,a/c\), for \(a = 10\,c\) ten times the weight. To the right of the lever the bar is drawn alone: the lever pulls it up with this force at the top, and the ground pulls it down with an equal force at the bottom.

In spite of the levers Musschenbroek could break wood and steel only when the cross section of the bar was small (TIMO, PDF p. 63). The force that breaks a bar is proportional to the area of the cross section, as Galileo found (TIMO, PDF p. 19). At fracture every small piece of the cross section carries the same force per unit area, as Galileo also assumed in bending (TIMO, PDF p. 20), so the sum of the forces of all pieces is proportional to the area. In the middle of the figure are a cross section of diameter \(d\) and a cross section of twice the diameter. The area of a circle is proportional to the square of its diameter, so the second cross section has four times the area and is broken only by four times the force that breaks the first. If the largest force of the machine lies between the two, the machine breaks only the thinner bar.

With bending tests of small wooden bars of rectangular cross section Musschenbroek confirmed Galileo's rule that the bending strength is proportional to \(bh^2\), where \(b\) is the width and \(h\) the height of the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 63). The bending strength here is the moment at which a bar built into a wall breaks. Why does the height count twice? Galileo assumed that at fracture the bar turns about the lower edge of the cross section and that the whole cross section pulls equally per unit area (view (2) of figure 1.16, TIMO, PDF p. 20). A cross section twice as wide has twice the area, so it pulls with twice the force and is twice as strong as the original one. A cross section twice as high also pulls with twice the force, but this force acts on a lever arm about the lower edge that is twice as long, so it is four times as strong. From the results on small bars Musschenbroek showed how to compute the ultimate load of large beams (TIMO, PDF p. 63).

Earlier experimenters usually measured only the largest force the bar carries, on the curve we will draw in section 3.1.3 only one point, \(M\). When iron and steel entered building and machine construction, this was no longer enough, because the properties of these metals depend on how they are made, and the largest force alone, without the rest of the curve, does not tell whether a metal suits a given purpose (TIMO, PDF p. 215). David Kirkaldy, for the firm Robert Napier and Sons, which had received orders for high-pressure boilers and marine engines where lightness and strength were most important, tested from April 1858 to September 1861 two new kinds of metal meant to replace wrought iron. The tests grew far beyond what was first intended, and in 1865 he opened a materials testing laboratory in Southwark, London (TIMO, PDF p. 215-216).

Kirkaldy sometimes drew marks on the bars and measured the distances between them after the test. In this way he showed that along most of its length the bar stretches uniformly and stays cylindrical, and only near the fracture is the strain larger and the cross section locally narrower (TIMO, PDF p. 216). We will draw such a specimen in section 3.1.4 (figure 3.13, bottom). Small elongations, after which a bar returns to its original length, he could not measure with short bars and crude instruments (TIMO, PDF p. 216). To measure such elongations accurately Eaton Hodgkinson used rods 50 feet long, about 15 m (TIMO, PDF p. 216).

Let us return to measuring the strain \(\Delta L/L\) on a bar. At the same strain \(\Delta L/L\) the elongation \(\Delta L\) is proportional to the length \(L\), and a longer elongation is easier to measure. The bottom of figure 3.9, which we will compute in section 3.1.2, shows two steel bars at the same strain \(0{,}00065\). A piece 50 mm long gets longer by only \(0{,}03248\) mm, a bar 10 m long by \(6{,}496\) mm, two hundred times as much. Both difficulties, the uniformity of the strain and the smallness of the elongations, are answered by the marks on the bar and a device that measures their distance, as we describe below (section 3.1.1).

3.1.1 The specimen and the measurement

The bar we test is called the specimen (preizkušanec). Usually it is a specially prepared round or flat bar (SADD §4.1, PDF p. 90). Often it has two thicker ends, the heads, between which there is a long thinner middle part of constant cross section, the reason for which we give below. The heads are clamped in the grips of a testing machine (preizkuševalni stroj), which slowly moves them apart and so pulls the specimen (figure 3.4). On the middle part we draw two marks at a distance \(L\), which is called the gauge length (merilna dolžina). A load cell (merilnik sile) between the upper crosshead of the machine and the upper grips measures the force \(F\) with which the machine pulls. An extensometer (merilnik raztezka) touches the marks with two knife edges and measures by how much the distance between them grows (SADD, PDF p. 90). The books we build on describe the test only briefly. The exact shapes of specimens and the procedures are prescribed by standards, which we do not treat here.

Why does the specimen have this shape (figure 3.4, right)? The grips squeeze the heads and pull them only over their surface, so near the heads the force is not spread evenly over the cross section, just as near the pins in figure 2.16. We therefore put the marks on the middle part, far from the heads. The middle part is thinner than the heads, so the stress \(F/A\) is largest there, since the same force is carried by a smaller area. If we load the specimen beyond the yield stress, it therefore gets permanently longer in the middle part, between the marks, and not in the grips.

From the measured force and elongation we compute the stress and the strain. In doing so we assume three things, each for a reason.

  1. The axial force in every cross section between the marks equals the force \(F\) of the machine. This is so when the specimen is in equilibrium and its weight is negligible (section 2.1). That is why the machine pulls slowly: in this way the specimen is practically in equilibrium at every moment. And the weight really is negligible. A steel middle part with diameter 10 mm, that is, with the cross-sectional area \(78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and length 50 mm weighs \(\rho g A L = 7800\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 \cdot 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2 \cdot 0{,}05\ \text{m} = 0{,}30\ \text{N}\), while at the yield stress \(220\) MPa the machine pulls with the force \(220\ \text{N/mm}^2 \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 17{,}3\ \text{kN}\). Because of the weight the axial force between the marks changes by less than \(0{,}002\) % of this force.
  2. Far from the heads the force is spread almost evenly over the cross section (section 2.2). Near the heads it is not: there the stress differs from point to point of the cross section, as near the pins in figure 2.16, and the quotient \(F/A\) would be only an average that holds at no point. How far is far, Saint-Venant's principle itself does not say. For a cylinder BOWER gives as a rule of thumb that the solution which ignores how the force is applied at the ends is applicable about three radii away from the ends (BOWER, PDF p. 230). Figure 3.5 shows the middle part of the specimen with diameter \(d = 10\) mm to scale, with the heads, which the force \(F\) pulls apart. Three radii are \(15\) mm, so next to each head we shade a band \(15\) mm long: in it \(F/A\) need not be the stress at every point. Outside the bands the force is spread almost evenly over the cross section, all arrows are of the same length. There we put the marks.
  3. The material is the same everywhere between the marks, so all pieces between them get longer by the same amount. Then \(\Delta L/L\) is the strain of every piece, not only an average over the gauge length. The assumption holds as long as the force of the machine grows. When the force reaches its largest value, the specimen starts to narrow at one place, and \(\Delta L/L\) no longer describes any piece: in our example in section 3.1.3 it shows \(0{,}30\), while in the narrowed part the strain is more than three times as large.

Then at every point between the marks the stress is \(\sigma = F/A\), where \(A\) is the area of the cross section of the middle part before loading (definition 2.6), and the strain is \(\varepsilon = \Delta L/L\) (definition 1.2). So the stress is nominal. For steel the area of the cross section decreases by \(0{,}06\) % at the strain \(0{,}001\) (section 2.2), so by less than a tenth of a percent up to the yield stress, and the difference from the force per unit area after loading is negligible. For large strains it is not, and these we treated in section 2.13.

We put axis \(x\) along the axis of the specimen and axes \(y\) and \(z\) across it (figure 3.4, right). Then the stress \(\sigma\) is the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the only nonzero stress component in a bar pulled by an axial force (section 2.6.6). The strain \(\Delta L/L\) is the normal strain in the direction of axis \(x\), which since section 1.17 we write \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). From here on we therefore write

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{F}{A} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} .\]

3.1.2 The straight line and its slope

The machine slowly increases the force, and at each force we write down the stress and the strain. Each pair of numbers is a point in the graph of stress against strain (figure 3.6): horizontally we plot the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), vertically the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in megapascals. For steel and most other materials the following shows up, as long as the stress is not too large (BOWER §3.2.1, PDF p. 96, SADD §4.1, PDF pp. 90-91).

  1. The points lie on a straight line through the origin, only measurement errors scatter them a little around it. The stress is proportional to the strain: at twice the stress the strain is twice as large, for example \(0{,}0005\) at 98 MPa and \(0{,}001\) at 196 MPa.
  2. When we decrease the force, the points go back along the same line, which the grey arrow with two heads shows. At zero force the strain is zero too, and the specimen returns to its original length.
  3. The strain depends only on the stress, not on how fast we pull and not on how the specimen was loaded before. In the graph this means that each stress has one single point of the line, whether we reach it from below or from above, quickly or slowly.

Above some stress the graph bends. If we unload the specimen then, for many materials it no longer returns to its original length. For steel this happens at the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) (definition 2.7, figure 2.23). SADD distinguishes three limits: the proportional limit (meja sorazmernosti), up to which the graph is a straight line, the elastic limit (meja elastičnosti), up to which the specimen returns to its original length after unloading, and the yield point, where large permanent strains begin. For many materials the proportional limit and the elastic limit are taken to be about the same (SADD, PDF p. 90). BOWER adds that the limit is hard to determine accurately, because the graph bends gradually (BOWER, PDF p. 142). All three limits and the whole further course of the graph up to fracture are drawn in section 3.1.3 (figure 3.10, points \(P\), \(E\) and \(T\)). Until then we stay on the line.

On the line the quotient \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is the same for all points. It is the slope of the line (section 1.3.2), that is, how much the line rises per unit of horizontal run. We denote it by \(E\). Figure 3.6 shows it with a grey triangle: over a horizontal run \(\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) the line rises by \(E\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). This slope is the number that tells how strongly the material resists stretching.

Why do the points lie on a straight line at all? The answer is in the structure of matter. Since Newton's time the elasticity of bodies had been explained by forces between the smallest particles of matter. Boscovich assumed that between every two particles a force acts along the line joining them, attractive at some distances and repulsive at others, with equilibrium distances in between at which the force is zero (TIMO, PDF p. 112). Let us draw such a force (figure 3.7). Horizontally we plot the distance \(r\) between neighbouring particles, vertically the force \(f\) with which they attract each other. The curve is schematic: it says only what Boscovich assumed. At the distance \(r_0\) the force is zero. This is how far apart the particles are in an unloaded bar. To the left of \(r_0\) the force is negative: two particles that we push closer repel each other, so the substance resists compression. To the right of \(r_0\) the force is positive: two particles that we move apart attract each other, so the substance resists stretching.

Now at the point \(r_0\) we lay on the curve a blue straight line that has the same slope there as the curve. Far from \(r_0\) the curve and the line part. Near \(r_0\) we cannot tell them apart in the figure, and the narrower the piece we look at, the less they differ (this is how we came to the slope of a curve at a point in section 1.3.2). How narrow a piece do we need? Below the yield stress steel stretches by at most \(0{,}00112\) of its length. If the bar stretches, the particles in it move apart by the same fraction, so the distance \(r\) changes by a little over a thousandth of \(r_0\) one way or the other. This is the orange window, which we had to draw far too wide to see it at all. In so narrow a window the curve is practically a straight line: the force between two particles is proportional to the change of their distance, as in a spring. The stress is the sum of such forces per unit area, the strain is the change of the distances divided by the distance, so these two are proportional as well. The same picture says why proportionality cannot hold without a limit: at larger elongations we leave the window, where the curve moves away from the line. This is a picture and not a derivation. A real substance has many particles in a complicated arrangement, and we do not get the number \(E\) from such a picture. We measure it.

From history

In his lectures of 1807 Young was the first to write down a number that describes how a substance resists pulling and compression, and he gave it by a column of the same substance, as we saw in chapter 2 (figure 2.15), but differently from us (TIMO, PDF p. 100). The weight of the column is to the weight that compresses the substance by a given amount as the length of the substance is to its shortening.

Let us return to the slope \(E\) of our graph and express it by Young's rule (figure 2.15). If some weight \(W\) compresses a piece of the substance of length \(L\) by the shortening \(\Delta L\), that is, by the fraction \(\varepsilon = \Delta L/L\) of its length, the weight of the column is \(W/\varepsilon\), that is, \(1/\varepsilon\) times larger. The weight \(W\) presses on a cross section of area \(A\), so the stress in the piece is \(\sigma = W/A\) and \(W = \sigma A\). On the line \(\sigma = E\,\varepsilon\). The weight of the column is therefore

\[\frac{W}{\varepsilon} = \frac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon} = \frac{E\,\varepsilon\,A}{\varepsilon} = E A ,\]

the product of the slope \(E\) and the cross-sectional area \(A\), as TIMO writes too (PDF p. 100). Young's column weight per unit area is therefore the slope of our graph. For \(\varepsilon = 1\) the weight of the column is just the weight \(W\) that shortens the piece by its whole length, and \(\sigma = E\): the slope \(E\) is the stress at which the substance would shorten by its whole length.

From history

In describing experiments of tension and compression of bars, Young found that the proportionality of force and strain, which Hooke had written down, holds only up to a limit, beyond which a part of the strain is inelastic and remains as permanent set, as the curved part of our graph shows (TIMO, PDF p. 100). For steel he estimated the stress at which the substance would shorten by its whole length from the frequency of vibration of a tuning fork and obtained \(29 \cdot 10^6\) pounds per square inch, which is about 200 GPa (TIMO, PDF p. 100).

TIMO does not say how the pitch of a tuning fork gives the slope \(E\) of the graph for steel. The reason is the same as for a weight on a spring (figure 3.8). A weight on a soft spring swings slowly, the same weight on a stiff spring makes more swings in the same time, because at the same displacement the stiff spring pulls it back with a larger force. A prong of the fork is a steel bar, attached to the stem, that bends to and fro. The bent prong is pulled back by the material itself, as a spring pulls the weight. A stiffer material pulls it back harder, so the prong swings faster and the pitch is higher. The mass of the prong plays the part of the weight: a heavier material speeds up more slowly under the same force, so the prong swings more slowly and the pitch is lower. For a known shape and the density of steel, the measured pitch therefore fixes \(E\). The calculation that says this with numbers comes in chapter 13 (GR (4.247), PDF p. 287).

The slope of our graph is thus the number that Young described with the weight of a column. So we give it a name.

Definition 3.1 Young's modulus (modul elastičnosti)

A bar of some material is pulled along its axis, which lies in the direction of axis \(x\), so that only the stress component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A\) is nonzero. Its strain along the axis is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \Delta L/L\). Let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) be proportional for all stresses up to some limit. Young's modulus (modul elastičnosti) of the material in the direction of the bar's axis is the number \(E\) for which, for all these stresses,

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} . \tag{3.1}\]

Source: BOWER §3.2.6 (PDF p. 102), SADD §4.1 and §4.3.1 (PDF pp. 91 and 95), CM (6.3.40) (PDF p. 267).

The modulus of elasticity is the slope of the line, a number with the unit of stress, since strain has no unit. Books also call it Young's modulus, after Young, who in his lectures of 1807 was the first to introduce the notion of a modulus of elasticity, but as a column of the substance and not as a stress (TIMO, PDF p. 100). It is a property of the material and not of the bar. For a material that behaves differently in different directions, however, it depends on the direction in which the bar is cut from the material (section 3.4). A bar of the same steel that is twice as long or twice as thick gives the same line, because the stress and the strain are already taken per unit area and per unit length. The number 196 GPa, which BOWER gives for mild steel and which we used without a name in section 2.2, is the modulus of elasticity of this steel (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). Now we see why the quotient of the stress and this number gave the strain there. We divide equation (3.1) by \(E\) and get \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\).

How can we picture such a large number? If we put \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 1\) into (3.1), we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\). So the modulus of elasticity is the stress at which the bar would get longer by its whole length, as with Young's column, if the line reached that far. It does not. Mild steel starts to yield already at the strain

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}}{E} = \frac{220\ \text{MPa}}{196\ \text{GPa}} = 0{,}00112 ,\]

where the line in figure 3.6 ends. This is approximately the thousandth from section 1.1 above which steel no longer returns to its original length. A larger modulus means a smaller strain at the same stress, so Young's modulus is a measure of the stiffness of the material (BOWER, PDF p. 102).

With Young's modulus we compute the elongation of a bar pulled by an axial force (figure 3.9). Let us draw the bar before loading grey dashed. Its length is \(L\), the area of its cross section is \(A\). At both ends it is pulled by the force \(N\), so the axial force equals \(N\) in all cross sections. The bar after loading we draw orange: it is longer by the elongation \(\Delta L\) we are looking for, and a little thinner. Let the stress be in the range in which the graph of the tension test is a straight line.

  1. By definition 2.6 the stress is the quotient of the axial force and the area of the cross section, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = N/A\).
  2. The stress is in the range of the line, so (3.1) holds. We divide it by \(E\) and insert step 1: \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E = N/(EA)\). Since \(N\), the area \(A\) and the material, that is \(E\), are the same in all cross sections, so is the strain: every piece of the bar stretches by the same fraction.
  3. By definition 1.2 the strain is the quotient of the elongation and the length, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \Delta L/L\), so \(\Delta L = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\,L\). We insert step 2:
    \[\Delta L = \frac{N L}{E A} . \tag{3.2}\]

CM writes the elongation of a bar in the same way (PDF p. 316). The formula stands on two assumptions. The first is that the axial force, the area of the cross section and the material are the same in all cross sections of the bar. We used it in step 2, where it gave that all pieces stretch equally. A bar made of pieces with different areas or of different materials we divide into pieces in which all three are constant, and we add the elongations of the pieces. In the hanging bar, however, the axial force changes: it falls from the weight of the whole bar at the top to zero at the bottom (figure 2.24), and the upper pieces stretch more than the lower ones. If we put the force at the top, \(N = \rho g A L\), into the formula, we would get \(\rho g L^2/E\), twice too much: the true elongation is \(\rho g L^2/(2E)\), and we will get it in section 3.1.10, where we compute point by point. The second assumption is that the stress is in the range of the line. Once the stress reaches the yield stress, the bar gets much longer than the formula says: for the steel of section 3.1.3, already at the stress 220 MPa, the yield stress itself, even by \(0{,}015\,L\) instead of \(0{,}00112\,L\), more than ten times as much. The elongation is proportional to the force and to the length and inversely proportional to Young's modulus and to the area of the cross section. We have met each of these patterns already. A bar twice as long gets longer by twice as much under the same force, as we found in section 1.1 for the bars of length 1 m and 2 m (figure 1.11), which is why \(L\) is in the numerator. A bar with twice the area of the cross section gets longer by half as much, because the stress in it is half as large, as with the two thin bars glued into one thick bar (figure 2.14), which is why \(A\) is in the denominator. We can also write the equation as \(N = (EA/L)\,\Delta L\). Under an axial force the bar behaves like a spring whose force is proportional to its elongation, with the spring constant \(EA/L\) (EP, p. 191).

Let us try this on the steel bar of chapter 2 with diameter 10 mm, pulled with the force 10 kN. The area of its cross section is \(A = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2\). The stress \(127{,}3\) MPa is 58 % of the yield stress, the orange dot on the line of figure 3.6, so we may use (3.1). By step 2 the strain is

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{N}{EA} = \frac{10\,000\ \text{N}}{196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2} = 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} .\]

The units cancel because \(1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N}/\text{m}^2\). In the graph this is the strain \(0{,}00065\) below the orange dot. If we make a specimen with gauge length 50 mm from this bar, the extensometer shows \(\Delta L = 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 50\ \text{mm} = 0{,}03248\) mm, a little over three hundredths of a millimetre. A bar 10 m long, like the hanging bar, gets longer under the same force by

\[\Delta L = \frac{N L}{E A} = \frac{10\,000\ \text{N} \cdot 10\ \text{m}}{196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa} \cdot 78{,}54 \cdot 10^{-6}\ \text{m}^2} = 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{m} = 6{,}496\ \text{mm} .\]

3.1.3 The whole curve to fracture

So far we have stayed on the straight line. What happens if the machine pulls on, beyond the yield stress, where the graph bends, and all the way to fracture? We need the answer for three reasons. A designer must know how much reserve steel has between the stress at which it starts to deform permanently and the stress at which it breaks. Whoever bends sheet metal or draws wire works above the yield stress all the time. And we understand the assumptions on which the line stands only when we see where they stop holding. The goal of this section is to read the whole graph of the tension test of mild steel, point by point and with numbers, and to say what the force and the elongation that the machine measures tell about the material and what they do not.

Let us take the same specimen as before: steel, round, with the diameter of the middle part \(d_0 = 10\) mm, that is, with the cross-sectional area \(A_0 = 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2\), and with the gauge length \(L_0 = 50\) mm. From here on the index 0 means the value before loading, because the diameter and the length will now change noticeably. The machine slowly moves the lower crosshead down. Slowly, because for mild steel the yield stress, the largest force and the elongation to fracture depend strongly on how fast it is stretched: in the tests that TIMO describes, the yield stress at the fastest stretching was more than half again as high as at the slowest (TIMO, PDF p. 305). Our numbers hold for a slow test. So the machine prescribes the elongation and measures the force. This matters: we will see that towards the end of the test the force falls, and a machine that prescribed the force could not measure that part of the graph.

From the measured force \(F\) and elongation \(\Delta L\) we compute as before: we divide the force by the area before loading and the elongation by the length before loading. Since we will soon meet another possibility, we give these two quotients a name and a symbol.

Definition 3.2 Engineering stress and engineering strain (inženirska napetost in inženirska deformacija)

Let the specimen have, between the marks before loading, the length \(L_0\) and a cross section of area \(A_0\). Let it be pulled by an axial force \(F\) that increases the distance between the marks by \(\Delta L\). The engineering stress (inženirska napetost) is the number

\[\sigma_0 = \frac{F}{A_0} , \tag{3.3}\]

and the engineering strain (inženirska deformacija) is the number

\[\varepsilon_0 = \frac{\Delta L}{L_0} . \tag{3.4}\]

Source: BOWER §2.2.4 (PDF pp. 71-72), SADD §4.1 (PDF p. 90).

The two quantities are not new. The engineering stress is the nominal stress \(N/A\) of definition 2.6, the engineering strain is the strain \(\Delta L/L\) of definition 1.2. On the line we wrote them \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). The name engineering says that we get them straight from what the machine measures, the force and the distance of the marks, without knowing what the specimen looks like at that moment. We use the index 0 as for the vector \(\vek t_0\) in section 2.13: the force after loading per area before loading. The engineering strain is one less than the stretch of section 1.1, \(\varepsilon_0 = \lambda - 1\), where \(\lambda = (L_0 + \Delta L)/L_0\).

Now let us draw what the machine measures if it pulls to fracture (figure 3.10). The graph is a single one, but we have to draw it three times, each time from at least ten times further away, because the line is so steep and so short that we do not see it in the whole graph. Young's modulus \(196\) GPa and the yield stress \(220\) MPa are from BOWER (Table 3.1, PDF p. 100, Table 3.9, PDF p. 156). The other numbers we chose for the example, of the sizes that mild steel has. The true values for a given steel come only from a test, since the plastic properties of metals depend strongly on composition and processing (BOWER, PDF p. 156).

Let us start at the top left, where the horizontal axis reaches only to the strain \(0{,}002\). From the origin runs the straight line with the slope \(E\) that we know. Its grey dashed extension shows where it would go if proportionality held on. On the curve we mark three points, the three limits of section 3.1.2 (SADD, PDF p. 90).

  • Point \(P\) is the proportional limit (meja sorazmernosti), here \(180\) MPa. Up to it the graph is a straight line. Above it the curve moves away from the dashed extension to the right: the strain grows faster than the stress.
  • Point \(E\) is the elastic limit (meja elastičnosti), here \(200\) MPa. Up to it the specimen returns to its original length after unloading. The letter \(E\) is here the name of a point, not Young's modulus.
  • Point \(T\) is the yield point, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa (definition 2.7). Here large permanent strains begin.

We spread the points apart in the figure to tell them apart. For many materials we take the proportional limit and the elastic limit to be about the same (SADD, PDF p. 90). Why we may is shown by three cases in figure 3.11. Each panel is a graph of stress against strain with the straight line up to the proportional limit \(P\).

  1. Let us take a point \(B\) below the proportional limit. On unloading it returns along the same line to the origin (property 2 in section 3.1.2), and there is no permanent set. So the elastic limit is not below the proportional limit. This follows from the line.
  2. That the elastic limit is not above it either does not follow from the line. A material could bend above \(P\) and on unloading return along the same curve to the origin, without permanent set. Then the elastic limit \(E\) would lie above \(P\), as in our sketch in figure 3.10. Some materials do have different limits (SADD, PDF p. 90).
  3. For iron and mild steel a measurement decided. Bauschinger had a mirror extensometer that measured strains of the order of \(10^-6\). As long as the elongations were proportional to the stress he detected no permanent set, and beyond the limit the elongations grew faster than the force. He concluded that the elastic limit of iron and steel may be taken equal to the proportional limit (TIMO, PDF p. 219). Steel that we load above \(P\) to the point \(B\) and unload therefore returns along a line parallel to the initial one, and a permanent strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\) remains (BOWER, PDF p. 142).

In the book we therefore idealize steel. We draw the line straight up to \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), and all three points fall into one at the strain \(220/196\,000 = 0{,}00112\). The error of this idealization is the horizontal distance between the point \(T\) and the dashed extension, in our sketch \(0{,}0012 - 0{,}00112 = 0{,}00008\).

What happens at the point \(T\)? Let us look at the top right graph, which reaches ten times further, to the strain \(0{,}02\). The whole left graph is now a narrow grey frame at the vertical axis, and the line is an almost vertical stroke. From the point \(T\) the graph runs horizontally: the specimen gets longer while the force does not grow. This part is called the yield plateau (polica tečenja). The material flows, hence the Slovenian name of the limit, meja tečenja, the limit of flowing. On our specimen the force on the plateau is \(F = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} A_0 = 220\ \text{MPa} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 17{,}28\) kN, and at this force the elongation of the gauge length grows from \(0{,}0012 \cdot 50\ \text{mm} = 0{,}06\) mm at the point \(T\) to \(0{,}015 \cdot 50\ \text{mm} = 0{,}75\) mm at the point \(U\), more than ten times as much.

The plateau is a peculiarity of mild steel. TIMO describes what happens in it more exactly (left panel of figure 3.12). The graph runs along the straight line up to the upper yield point. There the force suddenly drops a little, and then the metal stretches considerably at this lower stress, the lower yield point. C. Bach introduced the names upper and lower yield point for these two stresses (TIMO, PDF p. 304). We do not draw the drop in figure 3.10, because the force after it is only a little smaller.

As an explanation TIMO gives a suggestion (middle and right panels): the boundaries between the crystal grains of steel are made of a brittle material and form a rigid skeleton, which at a small stress does not let the grains deform permanently. Without the skeleton the graph would bend away from the line gradually. With the skeleton the material stays perfectly elastic and follows the line up to the point \(A\), where the skeleton breaks. Then the grains at once get the permanent strain \(AB\), which corresponds to the length of the plateau, and after that the material follows the usual curve \(BC\) (TIMO, PDF pp. 305-306). Copper and aluminium have no plateau, as we will see in figure 3.17.

At the point \(U\) the plateau ends and the stress grows again. The material that flowed has hardened: a larger stress is needed for further permanent strain. The phenomenon is called strain hardening (utrjevanje) (TIMO, PDF p. 303, BOWER §3.7.5, PDF p. 147). Why a metal hardens we say in section 3.1.7. How much, we see only in the bottom graph, which reaches to the strain \(0{,}3\). In it the top right graph is a narrow grey frame, the plateau a short horizontal dash, and the line can no longer be told from the vertical axis. This is the proportion worth remembering: the elastic part, with which this book deals, is the thickness of a line in the whole graph of steel.

From \(U\) the blackwhite curve rises ever more gently and reaches its top at the point \(M\), here at the strain \(0{,}20\) and the stress \(380\) MPa. This is the largest force the specimen carries, \(F_{\mathrm{M}} = 380\ \text{MPa} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 29{,}85\) kN, \(1{,}73\) times as much as on the plateau.

Definition 3.3 Tensile strength (natezna trdnost)

A specimen with the cross-sectional area \(A_0\) before loading is pulled in a tension test to fracture. Let \(F_{\mathrm{M}}\) be the largest force the machine measures during the test. The tensile strength (natezna trdnost) of the material is the number

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{M}} = \frac{F_{\mathrm{M}}}{A_0} , \tag{3.5}\]

the largest engineering stress during the test.

Source: TIMO (PDF pp. 305-306), BOWER §9.2.6 (PDF pp. 589-590) for the largest force.

The tensile strength is an engineering stress: the force divided by an area that the specimen no longer has at that moment. So it tells how large a force a bar with a given initial cross section carries, not how large a force per unit area the material carries. Standards write it \(R_{\mathrm{m}}\).

Beyond the point \(M\) the blackwhite curve falls. The specimen no longer gets longer uniformly: at one place it starts to narrow, a neck (vrat) forms, and all further strain gathers there (TIMO, PDF p. 306, BOWER §9.2.6, PDF p. 589). At the point \(F\), here at the engineering strain \(0{,}30\) and the engineering stress \(300\) MPa, the specimen breaks in the neck. This stress is called the breaking strength (porušna trdnost). The force at fracture is \(300\ \text{MPa} \cdot 78{,}54\ \text{mm}^2 = 23{,}56\) kN, a fifth less than the largest.

Let us collect the points of the graph in a table, with the elongation of the gauge length and the force on our specimen.

point name \(\varepsilon_0\) \(\sigma_0\) in MPa \(\Delta L\) in mm \(F\) in kN
\(P\) proportional limit \(0{,}00092\) \(180\) \(0{,}046\) \(14{,}14\)
\(E\) elastic limit \(0{,}00105\) \(200\) \(0{,}053\) \(15{,}71\)
\(T\) yield point \(0{,}0012\) \(220\) \(0{,}06\) \(17{,}28\)
\(U\) start of hardening \(0{,}015\) \(220\) \(0{,}75\) \(17{,}28\)
\(M\) tensile strength \(0{,}20\) \(380\) \(10\) \(29{,}85\)
\(F\) fracture \(0{,}30\) \(300\) \(15\) \(23{,}56\)

The graph leaves a question open. From \(U\) to \(M\) the material hardens. Why then does the force fall beyond \(M\)? Does the material soften beyond \(M\)? No. What falls is the engineering stress, which divides the force by an area that is no longer there. The orange curve is the true stress, the force divided by the area the specimen has at that moment (section 3.1.4). Up to \(M\) it rises to \(456\) MPa, and beyond \(M\) only a dashed arrow suggests it, because computing it needs the area of the neck, which we have not measured.

3.1.4 The engineering and the true curve

Let us look at the specimen itself (figure 3.13). In the top row is the middle part before loading, grey dashed, with the length \(L_0 = 50\) mm between the marks and the diameter \(d_0 = 10\) mm, that is, with a cross section of area \(A_0\). Four dashed cross lines divide it into five equally long pieces, so that we will see which part stretches by how much. In the middle row is the same part at the point \(M\), orange, pulled by the largest force. Its length is \(L = 60\) mm, \(\Delta L = 10\) mm more. All five pieces are equally long, \(12\) mm each: the strain is uniform. And the bar is thinner, with the diameter \(d\) that we will compute.

At every moment the force \(F\) is spread over the cross section as it is then, not as it was. The force per unit of current area is what the material really carries.

Definition 3.4 True stress and true strain (prava napetost in prava deformacija)

Let the specimen have the length \(L_0\) between the marks before loading. Let it be pulled by an axial force \(F\) at which the distance between the marks is \(L\) and the area of the cross section is everywhere between the marks equal to \(A\). The true stress (prava napetost) is the number

\[\sigma = \frac{F}{A} , \tag{3.6}\]

and the true strain (prava deformacija) is the number

\[\varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln\frac{L}{L_0} . \tag{3.7}\]

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 306), BOWER §2.2.4 (PDF pp. 71-72) and §9.2.6 (PDF p. 589).

The true stress is the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the Cauchy stress tensor, that is, the stress as we defined it in chapter 2, only that there for steel we were allowed to compute it with the area before loading. The engineering stress is the component \(P_{\mathrm{xx}}\) of the first Piola-Kirchhoff tensor (definition 2.119). The true strain is the logarithmic strain of section 1.1, the logarithm of the stretch \(\lambda\) (TIMO calls it the natural strain). Why a logarithm, and why the name true? We divide the elongation into small steps and divide each by the current length, just as we divide the force by the current area. Let us do this for our specimen, which stretches from \(50\) mm to \(60\) mm. In one step we get \(10/50 = 0{,}2\), the engineering strain. In two steps of \(5\) mm we get \(5/50 + 5/55 = 0{,}1909\), because we divide the second step by a bar that is already longer. It goes on like this:

number of equal steps \(1\) \(2\) \(4\) \(10\) \(100\)
sum of the steps, each divided by the current length \(0{,}2000\) \(0{,}1909\) \(0{,}1866\) \(0{,}1840\) \(0{,}1825\)

Let us draw these sums (figure 3.14). The horizontal axis is the current length \(\bar L\) from \(50\) to \(60\) mm, the vertical one the number \(1/\bar L\) by which we divide a step. The curve \(1/\bar L\) falls, because the bar gets ever longer. A step of length \(h\) divided by the length \(\bar L\) at the start of the step is \(h \cdot (1/\bar L)\), the area of a rectangle of width \(h\) and height \(1/\bar L\). On the left is a single step, of area \(10/50 = 0{,}2000\). In the middle are two steps, and the second is lower, of height \(1/55\), because we divide it by an already longer bar. Together they have the area \(0{,}1909\). On the right are ten steps of area \(0{,}1840\). The rectangles reach above the curve only by thin slivers, which shrink almost to half with every halving of the step: by \(0{,}0177\), \(0{,}0086\) and \(0{,}0042\) for one, two and four steps. That is why the sums settle at the area under the curve.

The sums approach the number \(\ln(60/50) = \ln 1{,}2 = 0{,}1823\), as we saw for another bar in figure 1.23. In the lectures this sum of ever smaller steps is written as the integral from \(L_0\) to \(L\) of the function \(1/\bar L\). We will define the integral in section 3.5, and there it will be exactly such a sum.

The machine does not measure the true stress and the true strain. It measures \(F\) and \(\Delta L\). We can compute them from these two if we assume two things.

Lemma 3.5 True stress and strain from the engineering ones (prava napetost in deformacija iz inženirskih)

Let the specimen have, between the marks before loading, the length \(L_0\) and a cross section of area \(A_0\), and at the force \(F\) the length \(L = L_0 + \Delta L\). Assume:

(a) the strain is uniform between the marks, so that the cross section is the same everywhere between them, with the area \(A\),

(b) the volume of the part between the marks does not change, \(A\,L = A_0\,L_0\).

Then the true stress and the true strain are

\[\sigma = \sigma_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_0) , \qquad \varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln(1 + \varepsilon_0) , \tag{3.8}\]

where \(\sigma_0 = F/A_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0 = \Delta L/L_0\) are the engineering stress and the engineering strain: the force on the initial area and the elongation relative to the initial length.

Idea

The volume of a cylinder is area times length. If it is conserved and the cylinder gets longer by the factor \(1 + \varepsilon_0\), the area must decrease by the same factor, and the same force on a smaller area gives a stress larger by the same factor.

Proof

We show both equalities from the definitions and the assumptions (a) and (b), on the middle row of figure 3.13.

  1. The length after loading is \(L = L_0 + \Delta L\). We divide by \(L_0\) and use (3.4): \(L/L_0 = 1 + \Delta L/L_0 = 1 + \varepsilon_0\).
  2. By assumption (a) the part between the marks has the same cross section \(A\) everywhere, so it is a cylinder and its volume is \(A\,L\). Before loading it was \(A_0\,L_0\).
  3. By assumption (b), \(A\,L = A_0\,L_0\). We divide by \(L\) and insert step 1: \(A = A_0\,L_0/L = A_0/(1 + \varepsilon_0)\).
  4. By (3.6), \(\sigma = F/A\), the force per current area. We insert step 3 and then (3.3): \(\sigma = F\,(1 + \varepsilon_0)/A_0 = \sigma_0\,(1 + \varepsilon_0)\).
  5. By (3.7), \(\varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln(L/L_0)\), the logarithm of the ratio of the lengths. We insert step 1: \(\varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln(1 + \varepsilon_0)\). This step does not need assumption (b).

Source: TIMO (PDF p. 306) for the definitions, BOWER §9.2.6 (PDF pp. 589-590), item 3 for \(\varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln(L/L_0)\) and item 9 for \(A = A_0 L_0/L\).

The proof used two assumptions, and we must look at each separately: why it is right here, when it holds and what it does to the result.

Assumption (b), the conservation of volume, is not a theorem. It is a fact of experience about the plastic flow of metals: the experiments of G. I. Taylor and collaborators on thin-walled tubes showed that plastic strains preserve volume (BOWER, PDF p. 143). We will see the reason in section 3.1.7: a crystal deforms permanently by layers of atoms slipping past each other, like the cards of a deck that we push sideways. The deck changes its shape, but there are no more and no fewer cards. The assumption does not hold for the elastic part of the strain. Below the yield stress the volume of a steel bar increases when we pull it, as we will measure in section 3.1.8. How much does this spoil the result? At the point \(M\) the elastic part of the strain is \(\sigma/E = 456/196\,000 = 0{,}0023\), against \(0{,}18\) of the plastic part. Because of it the volume increases by about \(0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}0023 = 0{,}0009\). We found the factor \(0{,}4\) in section 1.6 for a cube of steel, which at the strain \(0{,}001\) gets longer to \(1{,}001\) along the bar and shorter to \(0{,}9997\) across it, so that its volume increases by \(0{,}0004\), \(0{,}4\) times the strain. At the measured length the area is therefore also larger by the fraction \(0{,}0009\) and the true stress smaller by that much: \(455{,}6\) MPa instead of \(456\) MPa. The error is \(0{,}09\) %. On the line, where all the strain is elastic, we do not need the formula, because there \(\sigma\) and \(\sigma_0\) differ by less than a tenth of a percent (section 3.1.1). If we do not trust the conservation of volume, we must measure the diameter besides the elongation. For a round specimen this is the only additional measurement we need.

Assumption (a), uniformity, is assumption 3 of section 3.1.1. It holds up to the point \(M\) and not a step further. That is why the orange curve in figure 3.10 is solid only up to \(M\).

Let us compute it. At the point \(M\) we have \(\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}20\) and \(\sigma_0 = 380\) MPa, so by (3.8)

\[\sigma = 380\ \text{MPa} \cdot 1{,}20 = 456\ \text{MPa} , \qquad \varepsilon_{\ln} = \ln 1{,}20 = 0{,}1823 .\]

Let us check on the specimen of the middle row of figure 3.13. The area is \(A = 78{,}54/1{,}20 = 65{,}45\ \text{mm}^2\), the diameter therefore \(d = 10\ \text{mm}/\sqrt{1{,}20} = 9{,}129\) mm, and \(F_{\mathrm{M}}/A = 29\,845\ \text{N}/65{,}45\ \text{mm}^2 = 456\) MPa. We compute the other points in the same way.

\(\varepsilon_0\) \(\sigma_0\) in MPa \(\varepsilon_{\ln}\) \(\sigma\) in MPa \(A\) in \(\text{mm}^2\) \(F\) in kN
\(0{,}05\) \(274{,}8\) \(0{,}0488\) \(288{,}6\) \(74{,}80\) \(21{,}58\)
\(0{,}10\) \(333{,}3\) \(0{,}0953\) \(366{,}6\) \(71{,}40\) \(26{,}17\)
\(0{,}15\) \(368{,}3\) \(0{,}1398\) \(423{,}6\) \(68{,}30\) \(28{,}93\)
\(0{,}20\) \(380{,}0\) \(0{,}1823\) \(456{,}0\) \(65{,}45\) \(29{,}85\)

The orange curve lies above the blackwhite one and to the left of it: the true stress is larger than the engineering stress because the area is smaller than \(A_0\), and the true strain is smaller than the engineering strain because we divide the steps by a longer bar. At the beginning the curves coincide. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}00112\), at the end of the line, the formula gives a difference of \(0{,}11\) %. The real difference there is smaller still, because on the line the volume is not conserved and the area decreases by less than a tenth of a percent (section 3.1.1). So in the elastic part we do not distinguish the curves. At the point \(M\) the difference is \(76\) MPa, a fifth.

Now we can answer why the blackwhite curve has a top. The force is the product of the true stress and the current area, \(F = \sigma\,A\). In figure 3.15 all three quantities are drawn over the same axis of engineering strain: at the top the true stress \(\sigma\), in the middle the area \(A\), at the bottom their product, the force \(F\), the dots are the rows of the table. During stretching two things happen with opposite effects: the material hardens, so \(\sigma\) grows, and the bar gets thinner, so \(A\) falls. Let us read the last two rows of the table. From \(\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}15\) to \(0{,}20\) the stress \(\sigma\) grows by \(7{,}6\) % and \(A\) falls by \(4{,}2\) %, so the force still grows, from \(28{,}93\) to \(29{,}85\) kN, by \(3{,}2\) %. But the hardening fades, the orange curve flattens, while the thinning does not. At the point \(M\) the two effects are equal, and the force no longer grows (BOWER §9.2.6, PDF pp. 589-590, which calls the phenomenon geometric softening). So the material does not soften at \(M\). The true stress grows on, only the area falls faster.

The same calculation says why the specimen stops stretching uniformly at \(M\) (figure 3.16). No specimen is exactly equally thick everywhere. At a place that is thinner by a hair the same force \(F\) acts on a smaller area, so the true stress there is a little larger, and the place stretches a little more and gets a little thinner still. Before the point \(M\) this is not dangerous: with the additional elongation this place hardens more than it thins, so it carries more and the other parts catch up with it. At \(\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}10\), for a further true strain of \(0{,}01\), the area falls by \(1\) %, while the true stress grows by almost \(4\) % along the curve of the table, so this place carries almost \(3\) % more. Beyond the point \(M\) it is the other way round: the place thins more than it hardens, carries less, and so stretches even more. The strain gathers at one place, a neck forms, while elsewhere the specimen stops stretching and, because the force falls, even shortens a little elastically (BOWER, PDF p. 589: necking is usually unstable once it starts).

This is what the bottom row of figure 3.13 shows, just before fracture. The four pieces outside the neck are drawn as they were at the point \(M\), \(12\) mm long each. All the further elongation, from \(\Delta L = 10\) mm to \(15\) mm, went into the middle piece, which is now \(17\) mm long and squeezed in the middle to the diameter \(6{,}5\) mm. Assumption (a) no longer holds, and with it neither does assumption 3 of section 3.1.1. What does this do to the numbers? The engineering strain shows \(15/50 = 0{,}30\), but this is an average over the gauge length that describes no piece: four have \(0{,}20\), and in the neck it is much larger. In the narrowest cross section the area is \(\pi \cdot 6{,}5^2/4 = 33{,}18\ \text{mm}^2\). A short piece of material there has, if it conserves volume, grown longer by the factor \(A_0/A = 78{,}54/33{,}18 = 2{,}37\), so its true strain is \(\ln 2{,}37 = 0{,}86\). From the average strain \(0{,}30\) the formula (3.8) would give \(\ln 1{,}30 = 0{,}26\), more than three times less. The average true stress in the narrowest cross section is \(F/A\) \(= 23\,562\ \text{N}/33{,}18\ \text{mm}^2 = 710\) MPa, while the formula (3.8) would give \(300 \cdot 1{,}30 = 390\) MPa, almost half too little. Even \(710\) MPa is only an average: in the neck the stress is no longer uniform over the cross section and no longer uniaxial, it is largest at the centre of the cross section (TIMO, PDF p. 306, after the investigation of N. N. Davidenkov). That is why beyond the point \(M\) the orange curve in figure 3.10 is only a dashed arrow. We can draw it only if we measure the diameter of the neck during the test, and even then it is approximate.

Let us sum up when we use which measure. In the elastic part they are equal to a tenth of a percent, and this book computes with the engineering one. Between \(U\) and \(M\) the true curve says what the material carries, and the engineering curve how large a force a bar with a given initial cross section carries. Beyond \(M\) the engineering curve describes the specimen and not the material, and the true one can no longer be computed from \(F\) and \(\Delta L\).

3.1.5 The offset yield stress

Mild steel has a plateau, so the yield stress is clear in the graph. Most metals have none. For annealed copper or aluminium the graph bends gradually, and it is hard to say at which stress the line ends (BOWER, PDF p. 142). Wertheim took as the limit the stress at which the permanent strain reaches \(0{,}00005\) (TIMO, PDF p. 192). But a limit fixed in this way depends on how small a remainder the instrument still detects. Today we agree on a remainder that every extensometer measures reliably: \(0{,}002\), that is, \(0{,}2\) % (HK, PDF p. 319).

Let us draw the graph of such a metal (figure 3.17). The axes are the strain and the stress in MPa. The curve is an example we chose ourselves, for an aluminium alloy with Young's modulus \(70\) GPa (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100, gives \(69\) to \(79\) GPa): it starts as a straight line and bends continuously, with no plateau. The grey dashed line is the initial line with the slope \(E\), extended upwards. The construction has three steps.

  1. On the strain axis we measure off \(0{,}002\).
  2. Through this point we draw a blue line parallel to the initial one, that is, with the slope \(E\).
  3. Where the blue line meets the curve we read the stress. This is the offset yield stress, here \(150\) MPa.
Definition 3.6 Offset yield stress (dogovorna meja tečenja)

Let the graph of the tension test of a material be at the beginning a straight line with the slope \(E\). The offset yield stress (dogovorna meja tečenja) \(R_{\mathrm{p}0{,}2}\) is the engineering stress at the first point of the graph at which the engineering strain equals

\[\varepsilon_0 = \frac{\sigma_0}{E} + 0{,}002 . \tag{3.9}\]

Why a parallel, and why is this a sensible limit? Because the material unloads along a line parallel to the initial one (BOWER, PDF p. 142). So if we unload the specimen from the orange point, it goes back along the blue line and at zero force lands at the strain \(0{,}002\). The offset yield stress is the stress after which a permanent strain of \(0{,}2\) % stays in the specimen. Equation (3.9) says the same: the strain is the sum of the part \(\sigma_0/E\), which returns on unloading, and the remainder \(0{,}002\). Let us check on the curve of the example. At \(100\) MPa the strain \(0{,}00008\) stays after unloading, which is eight hundredths of a millimetre per metre of length, and at \(150\) MPa it is \(0{,}002\), twenty-five times as much. The total strain at the offset yield stress is \(150/70\,000 + 0{,}002 = 0{,}00414\), a little over half of it elastic.

When do we need the offset yield stress? When the graph has no plateau and bends gradually, that is, for most metals except mild steel. For steel with a plateau the yield stress is the stress of the plateau and the construction is not needed. What does the convention do to the result? Below \(R_{\mathrm{p}0{,}2}\) the material is not perfectly elastic, as the point at \(100\) MPa shows. Whoever computes with the linear elastic model up to \(R_{\mathrm{p}0{,}2}\) neglects permanent strains of up to \(0{,}2\) %.

3.1.6 The tension and the compression test

Instead of pulling a bar we can press it. In the compression test (tlačni preizkus) we put a short cylinder between two plates of the machine, which the machine brings closer together (figure 3.18). On the left the two tests are side by side on the same cylinder with \(d_0 = 10\) mm and \(L_0 = 50\) mm. In tension the cylinder gets longer and thinner: \(L > L_0\), \(d < d_0\). In compression it gets shorter and thicker: \(L < L_0\), \(d > d_0\). In compression the elongation \(\Delta L\) is negative, and so is the force, so the stress and the strain are negative too. Definitions 3.2 and 3.4 and lemma 3.5 hold unchanged, with a negative \(\varepsilon_0\). In compression too, however, the lemma needs assumption (a), uniform strain. In a real test it is spoiled by the friction at the plates, which does not let the ends of the cylinder spread, so next to the plates the material is compressed from all sides (TIMO, PDF p. 300). In a cylinder two to three times as high as its diameter the stress in the middle portion is nevertheless approximately uniform (TIMO, PDF p. 301). Our cylinder is five times as high as its diameter because it is the same as the tensile one, so that we compare the same numbers, and we neglect the friction at the plates.

What do we measure? BOWER reports: for a metal the stress-strain graph in compression is a mirror image of the tensile one, but only for modest strains. For large strains, changes of geometry cause differences between the two tests (BOWER, PDF pp. 142-143). Where the differences come from we can compute ourselves. Let us assume that the material behaves the same in tension and compression, that is, that the true curve is mirrored: at the true strain \(-\varepsilon_{\ln}\) the true stress is \(-\sigma\). This is an assumption about the material. It rests on BOWER for modest strains, below \(10\) % (BOWER, PDF p. 142), and our example, with the true strain \(0{,}0953\), stays just below this limit. On the right side of the figure we drew it orange, on the axes of strain and stress, with the curve of steel from the previous table.

Let us take the row of the table with \(\varepsilon_0 = 0{,}10\). In tension the cylinder is \(55\) mm long, the true strain is \(0{,}0953\), the true stress \(366{,}6\) MPa, the area \(71{,}40\ \text{mm}^2\), the force \(26{,}17\) kN and the engineering stress \(333{,}3\) MPa. Now let us press the cylinder to a true strain of the same size, \(-0{,}0953\). Its length is \(50\ \text{mm}/1{,}10 = 45{,}45\) mm, so \(\varepsilon_0 = -0{,}0909\). Because volume is conserved the area is \(78{,}54 \cdot 1{,}10 = 86{,}39\ \text{mm}^2\) and the diameter \(10{,}49\) mm. By the assumption the true stress is \(-366{,}6\) MPa, the force therefore \(-366{,}6 \cdot 86{,}39\ \text{N} = -31{,}67\) kN, and the engineering stress \(-31\,670/78{,}54 = \) \(-403{,}2\) MPa. The material did the same in both tests, yet the machine measured \(26{,}17\) kN in tension and \(31{,}67\) kN in compression, a fifth more. The blackwhite curves are therefore not mirror images: in tension the area falls and the engineering stress lags behind the true one, in compression the area grows and it runs ahead. At the strain \(0{,}001\), on the line, the area changes by only \(0{,}0006\), since the transverse edges of the steel cube of section 1.6 shorten to \(0{,}9997\) in tension and lengthen to \(1{,}0003\) in compression. There the blackwhite curves differ in size by \(1{,}0003^2 - 0{,}9997^2 = 0{,}0012\) of the stress, a little over a thousandth, and we do not notice the difference. That is why below the yield stress the same Young's modulus holds in tension and compression, and the same line, extended through the origin to the negative side.

The same picture says why there is no neck in compression. A place that is pressed a little more gets thicker, so it carries more and not less. There is no thinning to compete with the hardening, and the force grows throughout the test.

In the lectures we write \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ENG}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{ENG}}\) for the engineering stress and strain (our \(\sigma_0\) and \(\varepsilon_0\)), \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon\) for the true ones (our \(\sigma\) and \(\varepsilon_{\ln}\)), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{v}}\) for the yield stress (our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\)), and the stretch \(\lambda\) is called razteg.

3.1.7 The plastic response

We read the graph to fracture in one direction: the machine pulled all the time. What happens if we stop pulling above the yield stress, unload the specimen and load it again? Everyone who forms metal must answer this: a sheet that we bend straightens a little after unloading, and we must know by how much. The goal of this section is threefold. We will split the strain above the yield stress into a part that returns on unloading and a part that stays. On the simplest model we will compute why stresses stay in an unloaded body. And we will look into the crystal, where the permanent strain arises. The strain that stays after unloading is called plastic (plastična), after the Greek word plastikos, fit for moulding: the substance keeps the shape we gave it, like clay.

Let us draw the graph of the tension test once more, but only its beginning, and interrupt it somewhere above the yield stress (figure 3.19). The axes are the strain and the stress. From the origin \(O\) runs the straight line with the slope \(E\) to the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\), and above it the material hardens. In this sketch we left out the yield plateau and strongly magnified the strains, because otherwise the line would be too close to the vertical axis. At the point \(B\) we stop the machine and slowly reduce the force to zero.

Where does the point of the graph go on unloading? BOWER reports what we measure: during unloading the graph has a slope equal to the slope of the elastic part (BOWER, PDF p. 142). So the point does not go back along the curve by which it came, but along the blue line parallel to the initial one. Since this line is steep and the curve is gentle, the blue line reaches the axis far from the origin. The distance from the origin to that place is the strain that stays at zero stress, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\). The rest up to the point \(B\) is the strain that returned during unloading, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\). The two parts together are the whole strain \(\varepsilon\) at the point \(B\).

Definition 3.7 Elastic and plastic part of the strain (elastični in plastični del deformacije)

A bar of a material with Young's modulus \(E\) is pulled along its axis beyond the yield stress to the point \(B\), where the strain is \(\varepsilon\) and the stress \(\sigma\). Assume that the bar unloads along a straight line with the slope \(E\). The elastic part of the strain (elastični del deformacije) is the number

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{\sigma}{E} , \tag{3.10}\]

and the plastic part of the strain (plastični del deformacije) is the number

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}} = \varepsilon - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} . \tag{3.11}\]

So the strain is the sum \(\varepsilon = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} + \varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\), and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\) is the strain that stays when the stress falls to zero.

Source: BOWER §3.7.2 (PDF p. 145) for the split, BOWER §3.7.1 (PDF p. 142) for the slope of unloading.

The quantity \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\) is not new: it is the permanent strain of figure 2.23, to which we now give a name together with its complement. Let us check the split on our steel. Let the point \(B\) be at the strain \(0{,}02\), a little beyond the end of the plateau, where the curve of figure 3.10 gives the stress \(228{,}5\) MPa. At so small a strain the engineering and the true stress differ by \(2\) %, and we do not distinguish them here. Then

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} = \frac{228{,}5\ \text{MPa}}{196\,000\ \text{MPa}} = 0{,}00117 , \qquad \varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}} = 0{,}02 - 0{,}00117 = 0{,}01883 .\]

On the specimen with the gauge length \(50\) mm this means: under the force the marks are \(1\) mm further apart, after unloading they come closer by \(0{,}058\) mm, and \(0{,}942\) mm stays. Just under \(6\) % of the elongation returns. In the figure the elastic part is drawn about three times too wide, so that we see it. That a piece goes back a little after unloading is called springback (elastično izravnavanje) in metal forming, and BOWER lists it among the tasks for which we need models of plasticity (BOWER, PDF p. 35).

What happens if we load the specimen again? At first it follows the same blue line upwards, until the stress approaches the largest value of the previous loading. There the graph bends again and continues along the hardening curve, as if there had been no interruption (BOWER, PDF p. 142). So after the first stretching the material has a higher yield stress, in our example \(228{,}5\) MPa instead of \(220\) MPa. Bauschinger already noticed this: the yield point of mild steel is raised by loading the specimen beyond the initial yield point. If the second loading starts at once, the new yield point is the largest stress of the first loading, after a pause of several days it is somewhat higher still (TIMO, PDF p. 219). The curve that rises above the yield stress and the higher yield stress of material already stretched are thus two descriptions of one phenomenon, hardening.

Definition 3.7 stands on the assumption that unloading is a straight line with the slope \(E\). Let us look at it as at every assumption: why it is right here, when it holds and what it does to the result.

Why is it right? Because measurement confirms it (BOWER, PDF p. 142), and because the structure of matter explains it. We will see (figure 3.23) that in permanent deformation layers of atoms slip by a whole distance between atoms, and the crystal is then regular again. The bonds between neighbouring atoms are as before, so they respond to unloading with the same slope as before yielding. The stretched bonds relax, this is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\). The slipped layers do not slip back, this is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\).

When does it hold? Only approximately. An accurate measurement shows that unloading and reloading are not the same straight line but two slightly bent curves that enclose a narrow loop, called a hysteresis loop (histerezna zanka). Bauschinger found that a specimen stretched beyond the yield point is not perfectly elastic right afterwards and has a very low elastic limit on a second loading (TIMO, PDF p. 219). TIMO gives the reason: in the grains that are most unfavourably oriented, layers slip even before the average stress reaches the yield point, and this slipping during loading and unloading uses up energy, which widens the loop (TIMO, PDF p. 304). The average slope of unloading is therefore somewhat smaller than \(E\). With growing plastic strain and with repeated cycles it decreases further: if we stretch the specimen on to the point \(C\) and unload it, the slope \(E_1\) is smaller than \(E\), and in the next cycle \(E_2\) is smaller still. In the figure the difference is exaggerated: the blue dashed line with the slope \(E_1\) reaches the axis to the left of the grey dashed one with the slope \(E\).

What does this do to the result? Suppose the true average slope of unloading is a tenth smaller, \(E_1 = 0{,}9\,E\). Then from the point \(B\) the strain \(228{,}5/(0{,}9 \cdot 196\,000) = 0{,}00130\) returns instead of \(0{,}00117\). The plastic part is \(0{,}01870\) instead of \(0{,}01883\), the error is \(0{,}7\) %, and for the permanent elongation the idealization suffices. For springback it does not: the marks come closer by \(0{,}065\) mm instead of \(0{,}058\) mm, eleven percent more. Whoever must hit the angle of a bent sheet therefore measures the slope of unloading.

In section 3.1.9 we will draw the unloading of steel along a line with the slope exactly \(E\) (figure 3.34). This is the idealization of definition 3.7, and now we know what it is worth.

Why does anything stay in an unloaded body besides the permanent elongation? The answer comes from the simplest model that we can compute ourselves. TIMO says what we model: the grains in a metal are oriented differently, so some yield earlier than others, and when we unload the specimen, the grains that yielded cannot return completely to their initial shape (TIMO, PDF p. 304). We replace two such grains by two bars (figure 3.20, left). Bar 1 and bar 2 are equally long and have the same cross section of area \(A\). On the left they are fixed to a wall, on the right to a rigid plate pulled by the force \(F\). Both are of steel with \(E = 196\) GPa, but bar 1 has the yield stress \(220\) MPa and bar 2 has \(330\) MPa. Above the yield stress let the stress in a bar grow no more, as on the yield plateau. The model stands on two assumptions. The plate is rigid and stays vertical, so the bars always stretch equally and have the same strain \(\varepsilon\). Without it the weaker bar would stretch more, and the model would not describe grains that hold together in a metal. And there is no hardening. For our steel this is true as long as bar 1 is on the yield plateau, which reaches the strain \(0{,}015\) (point \(U\)), and we will stretch the pair only to \(0{,}0015\). Pulling further would harden bar 1. If at the strain \(0{,}0015\) it already had \(8{,}5\) MPa more, as much as the steel at point \(B\), the stresses that stay in the bars after unloading (step 4 below) would be \(33\) MPa instead of \(37\) MPa, with the same signs, and the conclusions would stay the same.

What does the machine measure? The force \(F\) that the two bars carry together. Equilibrium of the plate gives \(F = \sigma_1 A + \sigma_2 A\), where \(\sigma_1\) and \(\sigma_2\) are the stresses in the bars. The average stress, the force per the whole area \(2A\), is

\[\bar\sigma = \frac{F}{2A} = \frac{\sigma_1 + \sigma_2}{2} .\]

In the graph on the right we draw all three stresses against the common strain. We do the test in five steps.

  1. Up to the strain \(220/196\,000 = 0{,}00112\) both bars are elastic and have the same stress \(E\,\varepsilon\). The blue, the blackwhite and the orange line coincide.
  2. At \(0{,}00112\) bar 1 yields. We pull on to the strain \(0{,}0015\). Bar 1 stays at \(220\) MPa, bar 2 is still elastic and comes to \(196\,000 \cdot 0{,}0015 = 294\) MPa, which is less than its limit \(330\) MPa. The average is \((220 + 294)/2 = 257\) MPa. The orange line has a kink at \(220\) MPa and rises half as steeply, with the slope \(E/2 = 98\) GPa, because the stress now grows in only one of the two bars.
  3. We reduce the force to zero. Both bars unload elastically and, because of the rigid plate, shorten equally, so the stress in both falls by the same value. The force is zero when the average has fallen by \(257\) MPa. The strain decreases by \(257/196\,000 = 0{,}00131\), and \(0{,}0015 - 0{,}00131 = 0{,}00019\) stays. This is the plastic part of the strain of the pair.
  4. But the stresses in the bars are not zero. In bar 1 it is \(220 - 257 = -37\) MPa, in bar 2 \(294 - 257 = +37\) MPa. Bar 2 was elastic all the time and would like to return to its original length. Bar 1 is permanently longer by \(0{,}0015 - 0{,}00112 = 0{,}00038\) of its length and does not let it. So bar 2 stays stretched and compresses bar 1. The two forces are equal and opposite, and the plate is in equilibrium without an external force.
  5. Now let us press the pair, dashed. Bar 1 is already at \(-37\) MPa, so to reach its yield stress in compression, \(-220\) MPa, it needs only another \(183\) MPa. The pair yields at the average stress \(-183\) MPa and not at \(-220\) MPa.

Stresses that stay in a body on which no external force acts are called residual stresses (zaostale napetosti). BOWER describes them as a system of self-equilibrated stress that is established when a solid is loaded beyond the elastic limit and then unloaded (BOWER, PDF p. 238). The machine does not see them: it shows zero force, yet in each of the bars there is \(37\) MPa, a sixth of the yield stress of the weaker one.

The model shows three more things, and all three have been measured on real specimens.

  • The graph of the average stress bends before all the material yields. The orange line has its kink at \(220\) MPa although half of the material is still elastic. In a metal with many grains there are many such kinks and they are tiny (figure 3.21). Let us take more bars between the wall and the plate, with yield stresses spread evenly between \(220\) and \(330\) MPa, and draw the same axes as on the right of figure 3.20. The thin grey lines are the stresses in the single bars: each runs along the straight line up to its yield stress and stays there. Every bar that yields puts a kink into the orange line, because the stress now grows only in the remaining ones. With two bars there are two large kinks, with five there are five smaller ones, with fifty we no longer tell them apart, and the line bends continuously from \(220\) to \(275\) MPa. That is why the graph of a real metal with an enormous number of grains bends gradually, from the point \(P\) to the point \(T\) of figure 3.10.
  • During unloading the stress at some place can increase. When the average stress has fallen from \(257\) to \(37\) MPa, bar 1 is at zero stress. From there to the end of unloading the force still falls, while the compressive stress in bar 1 grows from zero to \(37\) MPa. So unloading a body is not unloading every part of it.
  • A metal that we stretched beyond the yield stress yields earlier in compression. In the model the limit in compression fell from \(220\) to \(183\) MPa. The phenomenon is called the Bauschinger effect (Bauschingerjev pojav), after Bauschinger, who measured on mild steel that stretching beyond the elastic limit in tension lowers the elastic limit in compression (TIMO, PDF p. 220, BOWER, PDF p. 143). TIMO explains it just as our model does, by residual stresses that add to the compressive load (TIMO, PDF p. 304).

The model has a limit that must be stated. In it unloading is exactly a straight line with the slope \(E\), because no bar yields in the opposite direction during unloading. When would one yield? We come closest to it if before unloading we stretch the pair until both bars yield (figure 3.22, left). The axes are the same as in figure 3.20. Then the average stress is as large as it can be, \((220 + 330)/2 = 275\) MPa. During unloading the stress in both bars falls by the same value, by as much as the average falls (step 3 above). So bar 1 drops by \(275\) MPa, from \(220\) to \(-55\) MPa, and bar 2 from \(330\) to \(55\) MPa. To reach the yield stress in compression, \(-220\) MPa, bar 1 would have to drop by \(2 \cdot 220 = 440\) MPa. The blue distance is shorter than the grey one, so bar 1 stays elastic.

In general: the weaker bar yields in compression if the average stress before unloading is larger than twice the yield stress of the weaker bar, \(\bar\sigma > 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}1}\). The average cannot exceed \((\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}1} + \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}2})/2\), so this is possible only if \((\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}1} + \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}2})/2 > 2\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}1}\), that is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}2} > 3\,\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}1}\): the yield stress of the stronger bar must be more than three times that of the weaker one, and we must stretch the pair far enough. On the right of the figure is such a pair, with the yield stresses \(100\) and \(400\) MPa, stretched to the strain \(0{,}0025\), where both bars yield. The average is \(250\) MPa, and bar 1 would have to drop by as much, the blue distance. But only \(200\) MPa separate it from its yield stress in compression, \(-100\) MPa. When the average has fallen to \(50\) MPa, bar 1 yields in compression, and the orange line has a kink already during unloading. From there it falls half as steeply, because the stress now changes only in bar 2. The average slope of the whole unloading is \(250\) MPa over the change of strain \(0{,}00153\), that is \(0{,}83\,E\), less than \(E\). In a metal with grains of very different strengths this happens, and from there comes the loop in figure 3.19.

The question remains what happens in a metal at all when it yields. We used the picture of forces between particles (figure 3.7) for the elastic part: the particles move apart a little and return. Permanent strain must be something else, because the particles do not return. On polished specimens of iron it was seen under the microscope that on the surface of some grains slip bands appear already at comparatively small loads: parts of the crystal slide past each other along definite crystal planes (TIMO, PDF pp. 303-304, the experiments of J. A. Ewing and W. Rosenhain). So the permanent deformation of a metal is shear, the sliding of layers of atoms, even when we pull a bar.

Let us draw this (figure 3.23, left). A crystal is a regular lattice of atoms. We draw the lower two rows blackwhite and the upper two grey, to see what moves. Between them is the glide plane, the grey dashed line. We load the crystal in shear: we push the upper part to the right and the lower part to the left.

The simplest thought would be that the whole upper part slips at once, like a card in a deck. Then all the bonds across the glide plane would have to be broken at the same time. A calculation of the shear stress needed for this from the forces between molecules gives enormous values, much larger than the measured ones. So it was concluded that sliding starts at a local imperfection and spreads from there over the glide plane (TIMO, PDF p. 303).

From history

In 1934 G. I. Taylor called such an imperfection in the arrangement of atoms a dislocation (dislokacija) and showed that under a small stress it moves along the glide plane and in doing so displaces one part of the crystal relative to the other (TIMO, PDF p. 303).

Back to the sliding of the crystal: the name of a dislocation says what it is: a place where the atoms are not at their positions, from the Latin dis-, apart, and locus, place. It is like a wrinkle in a carpet: we do not move a carpet by pulling all of it over the floor at once, but by pushing a wrinkle across it, and at every moment only a small piece moves over the floor.

Let us look at the middle picture. The upper atoms to the left of the blue sign have already moved by one distance between atoms to the right, those to the right of it have not yet. At the border between them the upper part has one vertical row of atoms too many compared with the lower part, and the lattice is distorted there.
