This is the dislocation: BOWER describes it as an extra plane of atoms inserted within a perfect crystal (BOWER, PDF p. 159). The vertical stroke of the blue sign shows this extra plane, the horizontal one the glide plane along which the dislocation moves. For it to move by one place to the right, only one row of bonds right beside it has to be re-formed, not all the bonds across the plane. That is why a modest shear stress suffices (BOWER, PDF p. 159).

In the right picture the dislocation has reached the edge of the crystal and left it. The whole upper part is displaced relative to the lower one by one distance between atoms, \(b\), and a step has formed at the edge. Above the glide plane and below it the crystal is regular again, and if we remove the shear load, the upper part does not slip back. One dislocation gives a slip by one distance between atoms. The elongation we see is the sum of very many such slips on many planes.

This picture explains three things that we only assumed or measured before.

  • Volume is conserved, assumption (b) of lemma 3.5. There are exactly as many atoms in the right picture as in the left one and they are equally far apart, only stacked differently. This holds for the slips, that is for the plastic part of the strain, and measurements confirm it (BOWER, PDF p. 143). Stretched bonds change the volume a little: at point \(B\) the bar stretches elastically by \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}} = 0{,}00117\) of its length and gets somewhat thinner as it does, so its volume grows by less than \(0{,}12\) %.
  • Unloading has the slope \(E\). The bonds in the crystal after the slip are the same as before it.
  • Yielding is set off by shear stress. BOWER states that a dislocation moves when the shear stress on its glide plane exceeds a critical value (BOWER, PDF p. 159). A bar that we pull has shear stress on oblique planes, largest, \(\sigma/2\), at the angle \(45^\circ\) (lemma 2.19, section 2.12). The glide planes, however, are fixed by the lattice of each grain (figure 3.24). The bar is pulled by the stress \(\sigma\), and in each of the six grains lines show the direction of its glide planes. The number in a grain is \(|\sin\theta\cos\theta|\), the shear stress on these planes divided by \(\sigma\), where \(\theta\) is the inclination of the planes from the cross section ((2.14)). In the grains with planes nearly parallel or perpendicular to the axis the shear is small, in the grains with planes close to \(45^\circ\) it is nearly \(\sigma/2\). So slips arise first in these grains (TIMO, PDF p. 304). We drew the grains in a plane, while real grains are three-dimensional. The numbers stay the same: the bar is the same all around its axis, so the shear stress on a plane depends only on the inclination of the plane to the axis, not on how the plane is turned about the axis.

With his model Taylor also explained hardening (TIMO, PDF p. 303). During yielding there are ever more dislocations and they block each other's way, so a larger stress is needed for further sliding.

The glide of dislocations is not the only way of permanent deformation. A crystal can also deform permanently by twinning (dvojčenje), in which a part of the crystal flips at once into a position that mirrors the original one. Amorphous materials, such as glass and many polymers, have no regular lattice of atoms and hence no dislocations in this sense. For polymers the response depends strongly on time and temperature (BOWER §3.6.1, PDF p. 131), and glass creeps slowly (BOWER, PDF p. 35).

How does all this enter the calculation? It does not. We do not compute the numbers \(E\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\) and the hardening curve from dislocations, we measure them on a specimen, point by point, and we choose the law so that it fits the measurements. Such a description is called phenomenological (fenomenološki), after the Greek word phainomenon, that which shows itself: it describes what we see from outside in a test, not what goes on inside. BOWER says this of all constitutive models: in general they cannot be calculated from fundamental physical laws, so they are fitted to measurements (BOWER, PDF p. 92). The branch of mechanics that computes the response from the structure of matter, from grains and dislocations, is called micromechanics (mikromehanika). A phenomenological description does not capture the mechanisms of deformation, so it holds only where we measured: at another temperature or another rate of loading the curves are different (BOWER, PDF p. 143). For practice it is nevertheless usually good enough. Hooke's law too, which we will build in section 3.2, is phenomenological.

What is still missing for a complete description of the plastic response? The graph of figure 3.19 holds for a bar pulled in one direction. BOWER lists what a theory of plasticity needs for a body under an arbitrary stress (BOWER, PDF p. 144).

  1. The split of the strain into an elastic and a plastic part. This is definition 3.7, the braces \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\), written for all components of the strain.
  2. A yield criterion (pogoj tečenja), which says at which combinations of the stress components the material yields. For a bar it is one point, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\). For an arbitrary stress we met one such criterion in section 2.12.6.
  3. A hardening rule (pravilo utrjevanja), which says how the yield criterion changes with the plastic strain. For a bar it is the curve above the yield stress.
  4. A flow rule (pravilo tečenja), which says how the plastic strain is distributed over the components. For a bar we do not need it, because there is only one direction. For an arbitrary stress the experiments show something unexpected: the increment of plastic strain has the direction of the stress, not the direction of the stress increment (BOWER, PDF p. 143, figure 3.25).
  5. An elastic unloading criterion, which tells whether the material flows on or unloads. For a bar it is the choice between the curve and the blue line at the point \(B\).

Let us draw what the flow rule says (figure 3.25). The axes are two components of the stress deviator, every point of the plane is one stress. The circle is the yield criterion: inside it the material is elastic, on it the material yields. The stress of a yielding material is the point \(S\) on the circle. The stress changes by the increment \(\Delta\boldsymbol\sigma\), which points obliquely, along the circle. The plastic strain, however, grows by the increment \(\Delta\boldsymbol\varepsilon^p\), which does not follow the oblique arrow but lies on the line through the origin and \(S\), in the direction of the stress.

We must add a description of how the material degrades while it deforms: voids form and grow in it, the stiffness falls, as the smaller slope \(E_1\) shows, and in the end it breaks. BOWER mentions the models that follow this as the most sophisticated (BOWER, PDF p. 35). We do not develop the theory of plasticity in this book. We stay below the yield stress, where the line and the number \(E\) suffice, and where, as we saw, the whole graph is only the thickness of a line at the vertical axis.

In the lectures we write \(\varepsilon^e\) and \(\varepsilon^p\) for the elastic and the plastic part of the strain (our \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{e}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\)), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{v}}\) for the yield stress (our \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}\)) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{v}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{v}}/E\) for the strain at the yield stress.

3.1.8 The bar gets thinner

When the specimen gets longer, it gets thinner at the same time. We described this for steel already in section 1.6: when a steel bar gets longer by a thousandth of its length, its thickness decreases by about \(0{,}3\) thousandths. Let us draw this (figure 3.26, left). The blackwhite rectangle is the part of the specimen between the marks, seen from the side, with length \(L\) and diameter \(d\). Axis \(x\) points along it, axis \(y\) across it. The orange rectangle is the same part after loading, and the grey dashed one is its outline before loading, so that we can compare them. The lower edge moves away by \(\Delta L\) and the length is now \(L + \Delta L\). Each side edge moves towards the axis, the two together by as much as the diameter decreases, and the diameter is now \(d + \Delta d\). In the test we also measure this, the lateral strain (SADD §4.3.1, PDF p. 95). We obtain it from the change of the diameter \(d\) of the middle part. The diameter lies in the direction of axis \(y\). Its change \(\Delta d\) divided by \(d\) is therefore the normal strain in the direction of axis \(y\):

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\Delta d}{d} .\]

The diameter decreases, so \(\Delta d\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) are negative. The blue length in the figure is therefore labelled \(-\Delta d/2\), so that it is positive.

In the range in which the stress graph is a straight line, the lateral strain is also proportional to the axial strain. In the graph we plot the axial strain horizontally and the lateral strain vertically. The points \((\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}, \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}})\) lie on a falling straight line through the origin (figure 3.26, right), as BOWER also draws them (Figure 3.5, PDF p. 97). The grey triangle shows its slope: over a horizontal run \(\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) the line falls by \(\nu\,\Delta\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), everywhere by the same fraction \(\nu\). The quotient of the two strains is therefore a constant number for a given material.

Why does the bar get thinner at all? The answer is in the bonds between the atoms (figure 3.27). Let us choose four neighbouring atoms at the corners of a square standing on its corner. Atoms \(A\) and \(C\) lie one after the other along the axis of the bar, atoms \(B\) and \(D\) across it, and the axes are as for the specimen. For small displacements the bonds between atoms behave like springs: a stretched bond pulls its two atoms together, a compressed one pushes them apart. We draw them as line segments, four oblique bonds with stiffness \(k\) and one transverse bond with stiffness \(k_{\mathrm{t}}\). The stiffness of a bond is the force the bond gives per unit of its elongation. When we pull the bar, the forces \(F\) move atoms \(A\) and \(C\) apart, each by \(u\). Orange are the new positions of the atoms and bonds, grey dashed the old ones. The oblique bonds get longer in this. A stretched oblique bond pulls its side atom towards itself, that is obliquely, partly also towards the axis. Atoms \(B\) and \(D\) therefore move towards the axis, each by \(s\). They are stopped by the transverse bond, which gets shorter in this and pushes them apart.

How large \(s\) is follows from the equilibrium of forces on atom \(B\) in the direction of axis \(y\), in three steps. Figure 3.28 shows the bond \(AB\) enlarged on the left and the forces on atom \(B\) on the right.

  1. The oblique bond \(AB\) makes the angle \(45°\) with the axis \(x\) of the bar, in whose direction the displacement \(u\) of atom \(A\) points. Of each displacement of its end only the part along the bond counts for the length of the bond. We get it by dropping a perpendicular onto the bond from the tip of the displacement. The displacement, the perpendicular and the part along the bond form a right triangle with the angle \(45°\), so its two legs are equal, and by Pythagoras' theorem the displacement, which is the hypotenuse, is \(\sqrt2\) times as long as a leg. The part along the bond is therefore the displacement divided by \(\sqrt2\). The displacement \(u\) of atom \(A\) lengthens the bond by \(u/\sqrt2\), the displacement \(s\) of atom \(B\) towards the axis shortens it by \(s/\sqrt2\), so the bond gets longer by \((u - s)/\sqrt2\).
  2. The bond therefore pulls atom \(B\) along itself towards \(A\) with the force \(k\,(u - s)/\sqrt2\). The part of this force in the direction of axis \(y\) is, from the same triangle with the angle \(45°\), again divided by \(\sqrt2\), so it is \(k\,(u - s)/2\). Atom \(B\) is held by two oblique bonds, \(AB\) and \(CB\), and together they pull it towards the axis with the force \(k\,(u - s)\). Their parts along the axis of the bar are opposite and cancel.
  3. The transverse bond gets shorter by \(2s\), because both its ends move in, and pushes atom \(B\) away from the axis with the force \(2 k_{\mathrm{t}}\,s\). The atom is at rest, so the pull towards the axis and the push away from it are equal and opposite:
    \[k\,(u - s) = 2 k_{\mathrm{t}}\,s , \qquad s = \frac{k}{k + 2 k_{\mathrm{t}}}\,u .\]

The quotient \(s/u\) tells what part of the stretching the thinning of this square is. Let us check it in the extreme cases. Without the transverse bond, at \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = 0\), we get \(s = u\): the side atoms move in by exactly as much as the axial ones move apart. For a very stiff transverse bond \(s\) goes to zero and the square does not get thinner. At \(k_{\mathrm{t}} = k\), as drawn, \(s = u/3\). The quotient therefore depends on how stiff the bonds are in different directions, and it can be different for every substance.

In step 1 we assumed that the bond stays at the angle \(45°\). This is right as long as the displacements are small: at the strain \(0{,}001\) and \(s = u/3\) the bond turns by only about \(0{,}04°\). If the equilibrium of atom \(B\) also takes this turn into account, \(s\) differs from \(u/3\) by less than a millionth of its value. For large displacements, such as those drawn for clarity in the figure, the angle changes noticeably and \(s\) is no longer proportional to \(u\): at the drawn displacement \(s\) is about \(6\) percent smaller than \(u/3\). The picture is also not a calculation for steel, since an atom in a metal has many neighbours in all three directions. But it tells where the thinning comes from: from the bonds that lie obliquely to the direction of the pull.

From history

Already Young, in experiments of tension and compression of bars, drew attention to the fact that a longitudinal strain is always accompanied by a change of the lateral dimensions (TIMO, PDF p. 100). In 1821, as we saw in chapter 1, Navier described the body with molecules, between which forces act along the lines joining them (figure 1.7). For a body that behaves the same in all directions he obtained with them a relation between forces and strains with a single constant (TIMO, PDF p. 113-114 and 189). How many constants are needed without molecules we say in section 3.2, and why molecules give only one, in section 3.4.

If a material is described by a single constant, for example the modulus of elasticity \(E\), materials differ only in it. The ratio of the lateral thinning to the longitudinal elongation must therefore be the same number for all such materials: it is a number without a unit, \(E\) has the unit of stress, and since there is no other material constant, the ratio cannot depend on \(E\). Poisson derived that in a bar of a material that behaves the same in all directions this ratio is always \(1/4\) (TP1, PDF pp. 252-253). The ratio was measured by Wertheim, who was born in Vienna and moved to Paris in 1840. In 1848 he pulled glass and metal tubes along their axis and measured how their internal volume changes (figure 3.29). This is the product of the area of the inner cross section and the length, so from the measured elongation and the change of volume it follows how much the cross section decreased, that is, the lateral thinning. The results did not agree with Poisson's \(1/4\), and the thinning could be explained only with two constants. Wertheim himself nevertheless kept one constant and proposed the value \(1/3\), without a theoretical basis (TIMO, PDF p. 192).

The number line shows Poisson's ratios. Poisson's result \(1/4\) and Wertheim's value \(1/3\) are two lines, and the measured values from the table later in this section are dots scattered between \(0{,}16\) and \(0{,}49\). The labels at the dots are abbreviations of the substances: SiO\(_2\) is silica glass, WC tungsten carbide, PA nylon, Fe steel, Cu copper, Al aluminium and R natural rubber. Nylon lies right on Poisson's line, while glass and rubber lie far from it.

Love in the fourth edition of his book of 1922 writes that the best experiments support the conclusion that the ratio can differ sensibly from \(1/4\) even in materials that may without cavil be treated as alike in all directions and at all points (LOVE, PDF p. 3 and 31).

So we do not derive the ratio of transverse narrowing to longitudinal extension from theory but measure it for each material. For mild steel it is \(0{,}3\) (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). The modulus of elasticity and this ratio are therefore independent numbers of a material in this book.

Definition 3.8 Poisson's ratio (Poissonovo število)

A bar of some material is pulled along its axis, which lies in the direction of axis \(x\), and let the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) be proportional to the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) along the axis. Let the normal strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) in the direction of axis \(y\), perpendicular to the axis of the bar, also be proportional to \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) in this range. Poisson's ratio (Poissonovo število) of the material for the bar direction \(x\) and the lateral direction \(y\) is the number

\[\nu = -\frac{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}} . \tag{3.12}\]

Source: BOWER §3.2.6 (PDF p. 102), SADD §4.3.1 (PDF p. 95), CM §6.3.4 (PDF pp. 264-265).

The minus in the definition makes \(\nu\) a positive number for materials that get thinner when stretched. For them \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is positive, because the lower edge moves away, and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) negative, because the side edges move in. Their quotient is negative, and the minus turns it around. Poisson's ratio has no unit, because it is a quotient of two strains. The Greek letter \(\nu\) is called nu. For mild steel \(\nu = 0{,}30\) (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). The number \(0{,}3\), which in section 1.6 we met as the ratio of thinning to stretching for steel and which stood in the displacement field of the hanging bar (1.19), is therefore Poisson's ratio of steel.

What other values tell us, we saw already in section 1.6. A material that behaves the same in all directions and keeps its volume at small strains has \(\nu = 0{,}5\). The volume of a round bar is the product of its length and the area of its cross section, and the area is proportional to the square of the diameter, since the cross section of such a material stays a circle (figure 1.106). The length is multiplied by \(1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), the diameter by \(1-\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), so the volume is multiplied by \((1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})(1-\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})^2\). When we multiply out and drop the terms with \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^2\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}^3\), what remains is \(1 + (1-2\nu)\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which at \(\nu = 0{,}5\) equals \(1\). At the strain \(0{,}001\) and \(\nu = 0{,}3\) the dropped terms are about eight hundred times smaller than the term that remains. For steel with \(\nu = 0{,}3\) the volume at the strain \(0{,}001\) grows by the fraction \(0{,}4 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}0004\), as we computed in section 1.6. A material that does not get thinner at all when stretched has \(\nu = 0\). For most materials \(\nu\) lies between \(0{,}2\) and \(0{,}49\), for metals around \(0{,}3\). There are also unusual materials with negative \(\nu\), which get thicker when stretched (BOWER, PDF p. 102). BOWER states that Poisson's ratio of every stable material that behaves the same in all directions lies between \(-1\) and \(0{,}5\), and that Young's modulus is positive (BOWER, PDF p. 102). What stable means we will say in section 3.6: to deform such a material in any way we must do work. From this we will prove both bounds there.

Why do we need \(\nu\) besides \(E\)? Young's modulus tells how the bar gets longer, Poisson's ratio how it gets thinner at the same time. For a material that behaves the same in all directions these two numbers will be enough to write the relation between all components of stress and strain (section 3.2).

For the steel bar with diameter 10 mm pulled with 10 kN we computed \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4}\), which is the elongation \(\Delta L\) divided by the length \(L\). By (3.12), therefore,

\[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = -0{,}3 \cdot 6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4} = -1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-4} ,\]

and the diameter changes by

\[\Delta d = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\,d = -1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-4} \cdot 10\ \text{mm} = -1{,}949 \cdot 10^{-3}\ \text{mm} ,\]

so it decreases by almost two micrometres, from 10 mm to \(9{,}998\) mm. Each side edge moves towards the axis by a little less than a micrometre. In the figure both changes are drawn about six hundred times too large, but their ratio is the true one. In a round steel specimen the contraction is the same in all lateral directions, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = \varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\), because steel behaves the same in all directions, and the cross section stays a circle, as for the hanging bar in figure 1.106. For a material that behaves differently in different directions, like wood, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}}\) can differ, and such a material needs several Poisson's ratios (CM §6.3.4, PDF pp. 263-265). We will turn to such materials in section 3.4.

The table gives Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio for a few materials (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). Where a range is given, the values for different kinds of the material differ. Wood is built of thin fibres that run along the trunk. These fibres are real threads of matter, not the imagined segments of definition 1.25. From the trunk we cut bar \(1\) along the fibres and bar \(2\) across them, both with the same length \(L\) and the same cross section, and pull them with the same force \(F\). Wood is stiffer along the fibres than across them (BOWER §3.2.8, PDF p. 103): bar \(1\) gets longer by \(\Delta L_1\), less than the elongation \(\Delta L_2\) of bar \(2\). The row for wood in the table holds for tension along the fibres, which is called along the grain.

material \(E\) (GPa) \(\nu\)
tungsten carbide 450 to 650 0,22
mild steel 196 0,30
stainless steel 190 to 200 0,30
copper 124 0,34
titanium 116 0,30
silica glass 94 0,16
aluminium and its alloys 69 to 79 0,35
wood along the grain 9 to 16 0,2
nylon 2 to 4 0,25
natural rubber 0,01 to 0,1 0,49

The values in tables are typical, not exact. SADD gives \(E = 207\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}29\) for steel (SADD, Table 4.2, PDF p. 97), because these are average values and individual materials differ somewhat (SADD, PDF p. 96). In this book we stay with 196 GPa and \(0{,}3\). Young's moduli differ between materials much more than Poisson's ratios. In the table the largest modulus, \(650\) GPa for tungsten carbide, is \(65\,000\) times the smallest, \(0{,}01\) GPa for rubber. Poisson's ratios, on the other hand, lie between \(0{,}16\) for silica glass and \(0{,}49\) for rubber, the largest only about three times the smallest. The two bounds given above allow this: Poisson's ratio is caught between them, while Young's modulus only has to be positive and has no upper bound. Figure 3.32 shows the lines of four materials on the same scale. At the same strain \(0{,}001\) steel carries a stress of 196 MPa, titanium 116 MPa, aluminium 74 MPa, wood along the grain only about 12 MPa.

Two materials in the table need a remark. Rubber has a Young's modulus in the table, but at the large strains at which it is usually used, for example in the rubber band of section 1.1 with strain \(0{,}5\), its stress is no longer proportional to its strain. Books therefore describe it with models in which the relation is not a straight line (BOWER §3.5, PDF p. 120). Its Poisson's ratio \(0{,}49\) has a simple cause. Rubber behaves the same in all directions, resists a change of volume very strongly but changes its shape very easily (BOWER, PDF p. 121). When we stretch it, it therefore almost keeps its volume, and a material that behaves the same in all directions and keeps its volume has \(\nu = 0{,}5\) at small strains. At large strains, for example \(0{,}5\), the ratio of the strains at constant volume is no longer constant, since then \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}} = (1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}})^{-1/2} - 1\) and the ratio \(-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{yy}}/\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\) equals \(0{,}37\). Wood, on the other hand, is stiffer along the grain than across it (BOWER §3.2.8, PDF p. 103), which is why the table gives the modulus only for the direction along the grain. For wood a single number \(E\) is not enough.

3.1.9 The idealized material

What we observed in the test we now write down as a model of the material. The model is an idealization: it tells how the material behaves, but only within the limits in which we tested it. It assumes two of the three observations from the beginning of section 3.1.2: that the stress depends only on the current strain (observation 3 says that the strain depends only on the stress, which on a line with slope \(E \ne 0\) is the same, since \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\)) and that it depends on it proportionally (observation 1, points on a line). The remaining observation follows from these two, as we will see right after the definition.

Definition 3.9 Linear elastic material (linearno elastičen material)

A material is elastic (elastičen) when the stress at every point of a body of this material depends at every moment only on the strain at that point at that moment, not on the rate of loading and not on how the body was loaded before. An elastic material is linear elastic (linearno elastičen) when every stress component is a sum of the six strain components, each multiplied by a constant number. In the tension test, in which only the stress component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) is nonzero, this gives the relation

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}} ,\]

where \(E\) is Young's modulus of the material.

Source: CM §6.2.1 (PDF p. 255), BOWER §3.2.1 (PDF p. 96), SADD §4.1 (PDF pp. 89-91).

What we saw in the test as observation 2 follows from the definition. As we unload the bar, the stress decreases, and at each stress the strain is again \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}/E\), the same as during loading. So the point goes back along the same line. At zero stress the strain is \(0/E = 0\), and the bar returns to its original length. CM calls a material whose stress depends only on the current strain and the current temperature Cauchy-elastic (Cauchyjevo elastičen) (CM §6.2.1, PDF p. 255). At constant temperature, which we assume in this section, this is our definition. In section 3.6 we will meet a stricter requirement, which concerns the work needed for a deformation.

The definition also tells us when a material is not elastic. The stress depends only on the current strain if every strain has a single stress. A material is therefore not elastic if there are two moments of the same bar with the same strain and different stresses. Let us take the same steel, \(E = 196\) GPa and yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa, but stretch the bar beyond the yield stress (figure 3.34, strain horizontally, stress vertically). Above the yield stress we idealise that the stress stays \(220\) MPa, which is only approximately true for real steel (figure 2.23). Unloading follows a straight line with the same slope \(E\) as the loading, as with real steel (BOWER, PDF p. 142). The conclusion below does not depend on the idealization of the horizontal line. For real steel the stress above the yield stress still rises, but less steeply than the line with slope \(E\). So the unloading line lies below the loading curve at every smaller strain, and the same strain again has two stresses.

We write out the definition for this case: a material is elastic if the stress is a single value at every strain. It is therefore rejected by one pair of moments with the same strain and different stress. We find it in the first three steps (figure 3.34), and the last two show that all three observations from the beginning of section 3.1.2 fail too.

  1. The yield stress is reached at the strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Y}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{Y}}/E = 220/196\,000 = 0{,}001122\). We load the bar up to \(\varepsilon_3 = 0{,}002\), which is more. Between \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Y}}\) and \(\varepsilon_3\) the stress is \(220\) MPa.
  2. We unload. The stress falls by \(120\) MPa, to \(100\) MPa, and approximately along the line with slope \(E\) (section 3.1.7) the strain decreases by \(120/196\,000 = 0{,}000612\). We chose the number \(100\) MPa as any example between \(0\) and \(220\). The strain is now \(\varepsilon_2\) \(= 0{,}002 - 0{,}000612 = 0{,}00139\).
  3. The strain \(\varepsilon_2\) lies between \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Y}}\) and \(\varepsilon_3\), so the bar was already at it during loading and had the stress \(220\) MPa. The same strain \(0{,}00139\) now has the stress \(100\) MPa, as the orange dot and the auxiliary lines from it to the axes show. The stress therefore does not depend on the strain alone, and the material is not elastic.
  4. The stress \(100\) MPa also has two strains: \(\varepsilon_1\) \(= 100/196\,000 = 0{,}000510\) during loading and \(\varepsilon_2 = 0{,}00139\) during unloading. At zero stress the strain is \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{p}}\) \(= 0{,}002 - 220/196\,000 = 0{,}000878\), not zero, and the bar does not return to its original length. The first sentence of this step rejects observation 3, that the strain depends only on the stress, and the second rejects observation 2.
  5. The quotient \(\sigma/\varepsilon\) is not constant: at \(\varepsilon_3\) it is \(220/0{,}002 = 110\) GPa and not \(196\) GPa. So the stress is not proportional to the strain (observation 1). This step alone would not reject elasticity: the quotient is not constant for rubber either, which is close to ideally elastic (BOWER, PDF p. 121).

For a smaller load the material would pass the test. If we load the bar only to \(0{,}001\) and unload it, it returns along the same line, and at every strain there is a single stress. Elasticity is rejected only by the path beyond the yield stress. The part of the definition that does the rejecting is the requirement that the stress does not depend on how the bar was loaded before: at \(\varepsilon_2\) the history determined it and not the strain alone.

Let us draw what the special case is. First the cube in the bar: in the tension test only the component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) on two faces is nonzero, the other components are zero. In a body there are six different components of stress and six of strain (the two columns of the table), and the general relation is a sum of the six strain components for each stress component (SADD (4.2.1), PDF p. 91). The tension test knows only one relation, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = E\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\). How we build the general relation from the tension test we will see in sections 3.2 and 3.4.

The second question is whether the material is the same in all directions. Figure 3.36 shows how we check this. From a block of steel we cut specimens in different directions. If in the graph they give the same line, the steel behaves the same in tension in these directions. With wood it is not so: a specimen cut along the grain is stiffer than a specimen cut across it, as the two lines show (BOWER, PDF p. 103).

Definition 3.10 Isotropic material (izotropen material)

A material is isotropic (izotropen) when its properties at each point are the same in all directions. For the relation between stress and strain this means: bars cut from the neighbourhood of the same point in different directions give the same graph of stress against strain in the tension test and the same Poisson's ratio. A material that is not isotropic is anisotropic (anizotropen).

Source: CM §6.1.1 (PDF p. 251), BOWER §3.2.1 (PDF p. 96), SADD §4.2 (PDF p. 92).

Why is steel isotropic, although it is made of tiny crystal grains, each of which behaves differently in different directions (BOWER, PDF p. 103)? The magnified view of a tiny spot in the block of steel shows the grains. The short lines in each grain show the direction of its crystal, and it is different in every grain. The grains are oriented at random, in all directions equally often, so in a piece containing many grains the differences average out (SADD, PDF p. 92). Specimens 1, 2 and 3 are much larger than the grains. Each cuts through very many grains of all orientations, so each has nearly the same share of grains of every orientation as the other two. This is the same reasoning as for the continuum in definition 1.1: the model describes the average over a piece that is large compared with the grains and small compared with the body (BOWER, PDF p. 93). The average fails when the orientations are no longer equally frequent. When the grains line up in a preferred direction during the processing of a metal, the metal is anisotropic too (BOWER, PDF p. 103). It also fails for a piece so small that it contains only a few grains.

The third question is whether the material is the same at all points of the body. We check this too with specimens cut from different parts of the body in the same direction (figure 3.38). From a block of steel we cut horizontal specimen 1 near the top and 2 near the bottom. If in the graph they give the same line, the steel behaves the same in tension at both points. With a column of soil, whose properties depend on depth (SADD, PDF p. 92), it is not so: specimens 1 and 2 at different depths give in the graph different lines, as drawn for the example.

Definition 3.11 Homogeneous material (homogen material)

The material of a body is homogeneous (homogen) when its properties are the same at all points of the body, that is, they do not depend on the position of the point. For the relation between stress and strain this means: bars cut from different parts of the body in the same direction give the same graph of stress against strain in the tension test and the same Poisson's ratio.

Source: CM §6.1.1 (PDF p. 251), SADD §4.2 (PDF p. 92).

Isotropy concerns the directions at one point, homogeneity different points. The two properties are independent: a material can be homogeneous and anisotropic, or isotropic and inhomogeneous (CM, PDF p. 251). Figure 3.37 shows all four possibilities, each square a magnified piece of a different material. We compare directions as with the specimens of steel and wood, direction 1 horizontal, direction 2 vertical, and places at point \(A\) near the top and point \(B\) near the bottom. For the example we assume that the particles and fibres are stiffer than the substance between them, so the material is stiffer where there are more of them. The round particles on the left have no direction. They are placed at random, so in a piece containing many particles the differences between directions average out as with the grains of steel, and in the left column \(E_1 = E_2\). On the right the fibres are horizontal and give the material a preferred direction. Along them the material is stiffer than across them, as with wood, so in the right column \(E_1 \ne E_2\).

In the top row there are as many particles or fibres at \(A\) as at \(B\), so \(E_{\mathrm{A}} = E_{\mathrm{B}}\). In the bottom row there are more of them deeper down, so the material is stiffer at \(B\) than at \(A\), \(E_{\mathrm{A}} \ne E_{\mathrm{B}}\). A material whose composition changes with position is also made on purpose, for example by powder metallurgy, and is called a functionally graded material (funkcijsko gradientni material), graded because its composition changes gradually with position (SADD, PDF p. 92). Since each of the four squares is possible, neither property follows from the other. In the bottom row the specimens must be short compared with the distance over which the density changes noticeably. A vertical specimen from \(A\) to \(B\) would average the sparse and the dense part and show a difference that does not come from the direction.

The properties of soil depend on the depth below the surface, so soil is not homogeneous (SADD, PDF p. 92, figure 3.38, middle). For a homogeneous isotropic material \(E\) and \(\nu\) are two numbers for the whole body, for an inhomogeneous one they would depend on the position of the point.

Let us also show what homogeneity rejects (figure 3.38, bottom). We glue a block from two parts, ordinary structural steel with \(E = 196\) GPa on top and stainless steel with \(E = 190\) GPa below (the lower end of the range in the table in section 3.1.2), both isotropic with \(\nu = 0{,}30\). The material of the body is not homogeneous if there are two bars from its different parts in the same direction that give different graphs of stress or different Poisson's ratios. We cut out two horizontal bars, one from the upper part and one from the lower. At the strain \(0{,}001\) the stress in the first is \(196 \cdot 0{,}001 = 0{,}196\) GPa \(= 196\) MPa, and in the second \(190\) MPa. The graphs are different lines, which at this strain differ by \(6\) MPa. Their slopes differ by \(6\) GPa or \(3\) percent (\(6/196 = 0{,}031\)). The Poisson's ratios are equal, so the different graph alone rejects homogeneity, although each part by itself is isotropic and homogeneous. A difference of \(3\) percent is small and can be neglected in the calculation of a structure, but this is a simplification of the model: if we compute the whole block with \(196\) GPa, we get the elongation of the lower part at a given stress in it \(3\) percent too small. The definition requires the same graph and not approximately the same one. If the whole block were of structural steel, all the specimens would give a line with slope \(196\) GPa, as in the figure, top.

The model we will use in this chapter and in most of the book is a linear elastic, isotropic and homogeneous material. It is described by two numbers, \(E\) and \(\nu\). For steel structures and machine parts it is a good model, but only under the conditions in which we measured it. Let us list them, each with the limit where it fails.

  1. Small strains. We computed the stress with the area of the cross section before loading and the strain as \(\Delta L/L\). When the strains are small, it does not matter which area and which strain measure we use (BOWER, PDF p. 96). For steel below the yield stress the diameter of the cross section decreases at most by the fraction \(\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{Y}} = 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}001122\), and the area by \(1 - (1 - 0{,}3 \cdot 0{,}001122)^2 = 0{,}00067\), so by less than a tenth of a percent. By this much the stress on the actual cross section is larger than the computed one. The strain measures of section 1.1 differ by half a permille at the strain \(0{,}001\), near the origin. For the rubber band with strain \(0{,}5\) this is not so, and then we need the stresses of section 2.13.
  2. Stresses in the range of the line. Above the yield stress a permanent strain remains after unloading (figure 2.23), and the material is no longer elastic. How far off the model is there, figure 3.39 shows: strain horizontally, stress in MPa vertically. Up to the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa the model and the bar follow the same line, above it the bar continues horizontally, as we idealized it above. The model extends the line with slope \(E = 196\) GPa beyond the yield stress. At the strain \(0{,}002\) it predicts the stress \(196\,000 \cdot 0{,}002 = 392\) MPa, while the bar carries only \(220\) MPa. The difference is \(172\) MPa: the model overestimates the stress by \(78\) percent (\(172/220 = 0{,}78\)), for real steel, which still hardens above the yield stress, by somewhat less. Such behaviour is described by other models (BOWER §3.7, PDF pp. 142-156).
  1. Slow loading. We did the test slowly, so that the specimen was in equilibrium at every moment. BOWER states that at sufficiently small stresses the strain of almost any material does not depend on the rate of loading (BOWER, PDF p. 96), so the line stays the same in a fast and in a slow test. For polymers such as nylon, however, the behaviour often depends strongly on the rate of loading, on the temperature and on earlier loadings (BOWER §3.5, PDF p. 120). Such materials are called viscoelastic (viskoelastični), and we will meet them in chapter 20.
  2. Constant temperature. A heated bar gets longer even without a force (BOWER, PDF p. 96). Steel heated by 1 K gets longer by about \(15\) millionths of its length (BOWER, Table 3.1, PDF p. 100). How much that is, let us compare on our steel bar with diameter 10 mm (figure 3.40). We fix two such bars with their left ends to a wall, the right end is free. We heat the upper one by 10 K without a force, and after heating it is longer by \(10 \cdot 15 \cdot 10^{-6} = 1{,}5 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of its length. The lower one is pulled at the original temperature by the force 10 kN, which stretches it by \(6{,}496 \cdot 10^{-4}\) of its length. Both changes are magnified by the same factor. The elongation from heating is thus almost a quarter of the elongation from the force, \(1{,}5/6{,}496 = 0{,}23\), although we heated the bar by only 10 K. We will add this part of the strain in section 3.3. The modulus itself can also depend on the temperature. Rubber gets stiffer when heated, which is just the opposite of metals (BOWER, PDF p. 121).
  1. Isotropy and homogeneity. Isotropy does not hold for wood, for fibre-reinforced composites and for single crystals (BOWER, PDF p. 103), homogeneity not for soil, whose stiffness changes with depth (SADD, PDF p. 92). We will treat anisotropic materials in section 3.4.

3.1.10 The hanging bar to the end

Now we can finish the computation we have owed since chapter 1. A steel bar of length \(L = 10\) m with a round cross section of diameter 10 mm hangs under its own weight. The density of steel is \(\rho = 7800\) kg/m³, the gravitational acceleration \(g = 9{,}81\) m/s². The bar is held in the idealized way described in section 1.7.1: only the point \(O\) at the centre of the top face is fixed, and the top face is pulled up by a force spread evenly over it. The axis \(x\) points vertically down from \(O\), and the coordinate \(x\) is the depth of a point below the top face before loading. In section 2.2 we computed from equilibrium the stress in the cross section at the depth \(x\),

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x) = \rho g\,(L - x) .\]

From it we want to compute the strain and the displacement of the points on the axis of the bar, which in section 1.2 we took from the books.

Which model do we use? Let steel be a linear elastic, isotropic and homogeneous material with modulus \(E = 196\) GPa. The stress at the top, \(\rho g L = 0{,}765\) MPa, is 288 times smaller than the yield stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{Y}} = 220\) MPa, so we are far inside the range of the line. But we need one more assumption, because the stress in the hanging bar changes with depth, while in the specimen it was the same everywhere. We assume that the stress at a point depends only on the strain of the material close to that point (BOWER, PDF p. 93). The relation (3.1), measured on a specimen in which stress and strain are the same everywhere, then holds at each point separately. The assumption is an approximation. At the scale of atoms and of the grains, the tiny crystals that steel is made of, the material is not the same everywhere. So the relation describes the average stress and strain in a piece that is larger than the grains and small compared with the bar, and it does not hold for a piece that holds only a few grains (BOWER, PDF p. 93).

Is this assumption sensible for the hanging bar? On the left of the figure is the hanging bar, held by an even pull on its top face, with only the point \(O\) fixed and the axis \(x\) pointing down. A short piece of the bar between the depths \(x\) and \(x + \Delta x\) is loaded like a small specimen pulled by two forces \(F\) (figure 3.41). In the middle the piece is enlarged. The part of the bar above pulls it up with the force \(N(x)\), the part below pulls it down with the force \(N(x + \Delta x)\). Nothing pulls it or squeezes it sideways, since the only nonzero stress component in the bar is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) (CM Example 7.3.2, PDF p. 305). The only difference from a specimen is the weight of the piece, \(\rho g A\,\Delta x\), by which \(N(x)\) is larger than \(N(x + \Delta x)\).

How large the weight of the piece is compared with the force \(N(x)\) is shown in figure 3.42 with three equal hanging bars, each with a different piece. The bar is equally thick everywhere and made of the same steel, so the weight of each of its parts is proportional to its length. The force \(N(x)\) holds the whole part of the bar below the depth \(x\), so by the equilibrium of this part it equals its weight, \(N(x) = \rho g A\,(L - x)\) (section 2.2). It is represented by the length \(L - x\) from the piece to the bottom. The weight of the piece is \(N(x) - N(x + \Delta x) = \rho g A\,\Delta x\), represented by the length of the piece \(\Delta x\). Their ratio is

\[\frac{\rho g A\,\Delta x}{\rho g A\,(L - x)} = \frac{\Delta x}{L - x} .\]

For a piece of length \(1\) cm at the top of a bar \(10\) m long this is \(0{,}01/10 = 0{,}001\), a thousandth. At every depth \(x < L\) the ratio goes to zero as the piece gets shorter, so we take the limit at each depth separately. Near the bottom, where only \(5\) cm of the bar are left below the piece, the same piece of length \(1\) cm gives the ratio \(0{,}01/0{,}05 = 0{,}2\), two hundred times more than at the top. There we shorten the piece more: a piece of length \(0{,}05\) mm gives a thousandth again.

The computation goes in steps.

  1. The stress at the point on the axis at the depth \(x\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x) = \rho g\,(L - x)\), largest at the top and zero at the bottom.
  2. By (3.1), applied at this point, the strain there is
    \[\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(x) = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}(x)}{E} = \frac{\rho g\,(L - x)}{E} . \tag{3.13}\]
    At the top, at \(x = 0\), this is \(\rho g L/E = 765\,180\ \text{Pa}/(196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}) = 3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-6}\), the number from section 2.2.
  3. The strain at a point is the derivative of the displacement, \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(x) = u'(x)\) (definition 1.10). At the top, at \(x = 0\), and at the bottom, at \(x = L\), this is a one-sided derivative (definition 1.9), since we know the displacement only on the bar, for \(x\) from \(0\) to \(L\). When the displacement is a polynomial, which has an ordinary derivative at the end point, this derivative is also the one-sided one, because a limit on both sides of zero is also a limit from one side (section 1.3.3). So we look for a function \(u\) whose derivative is (3.13) and whose value at the top is \(u(0) = 0\), because the point \(O\) is fixed.
  4. By lemma 1.82 on the rules of differentiation, the derivative of the function \(x\) is \(1\), the derivative of the function \(x^2\) is \(2x\), the derivative of a sum is the sum of the derivatives and the derivative of a multiple is the multiple of the derivative. The function
    \[u(x) = \frac{\rho g L}{E}\,x - \frac{\rho g}{2E}\,x^2\]
    therefore has the derivative \(\rho g L/E - (\rho g/(2E)) \cdot 2x = \rho g\,(L - x)/E\), which is (3.13). We chose the factor \(\tfrac12\) in front of \(x^2\) precisely so that it cancels the \(2\) from the derivative \(2x\). The graph of this function is the edge of the displacement shape.
  5. At \(x = 0\) both terms are zero, so \(u(0) = 0\), as step 3 requires. We take out \(\rho g/(2E)\) and get
    \[u(x) = \frac{\rho g}{2E}\,(2Lx - x^2) . \tag{3.14}\]
  6. There is no other such function. Let \(v\) be any function that is continuous on \([0, L]\), has the derivative (3.13) on \((0, L)\) and satisfies \(v(0) = 0\). The function \(u\) is a polynomial, so it is continuous, and \(v\) is continuous by assumption. The difference \(w = u - v\) is therefore continuous on \([0, L]\) by corollary 1.65 on the sum and product of continuous functions, and by the lemma on the rules of differentiation it has the derivative \(u' - v' = 0\) on \((0, L)\). In the displacement diagram this means: the edge of the shape starts at zero at the top, and at each depth the width of the strain shape prescribes its derivative, so there is no other way for it to go.
  7. Take any \(x\) in \((0, L]\). By the mean value theorem (theorem 1.85), applied to \(w\) on \([0, x]\), there is a \(\xi\) between \(0\) and \(x\) with \(w(x) - w(0) = w'(\xi)\,(x - 0)\). In figure 1.331 this is the interval \([a, t]\) with the point \(\xi\), for \(a = 0\) and \(t = x\). Since \(w'(\xi) = 0\), we get \(w(x) = w(0) = u(0) - v(0) = 0\), so \(v(x) = u(x)\): every such function has the same edge of the displacement shape. Steps 6 and 7 repeat the proof of corollary 1.86 on a function with zero derivative for the function \(w\).

Let us compare with section 1.2, where we took \(u(x) = a\,(2Lx - x^2)\). The two formulas agree if

\[a = \frac{\rho g}{2E} = \frac{7800\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2}{2 \cdot 196 \cdot 10^9\ \text{Pa}} = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-7}\ \text{m}^{-1} ,\]

which is exactly the number from chapter 1 (BARBER (1.33), (1.34), (1.38), (1.39), PDF pp. 32-34). The unit is right. The numerator is in \(\text{kg}/(\text{m}^2\,\text{s}^2)\), the denominator in \(\text{Pa} = \text{kg}/(\text{m}\,\text{s}^2)\), and the quotient is \(1/\text{m}\). The constant \(a\), of which we said there that it depends only on how heavy steel is and how strongly it resists stretching, is therefore the weight per unit volume of steel, \(\rho g\), divided by twice Young's modulus. The two in the denominator comes from step 4: the derivative of the function \(2Lx - x^2\) is \(2\,(L - x)\), while the derivative of the displacement must be \(\rho g\,(L - x)/E\).

The result holds under the assumptions of the model and for the idealized holding of the bar. Near a real ceiling to which the bar is welded the field is somewhat different. In our model the edge of the top face moves towards the axis by \(5{,}856 \cdot 10^{-9}\) m, but the weld does not let it. Lower down the two fields are nearly the same (section 1.7.1, SADD §5.6, PDF pp. 114-115). Figure 3.43 shows the stress, the strain and the displacement along the bar. The lower end moves by \(u(L) = \rho g L^2/(2E) = 1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, as in section 1.4. At the depth \(L/2 = 5\) m the displacement is

\[u(L/2) = a\,\Big(2L \cdot \frac{L}{2} - \frac{L^2}{4}\Big) = \frac34\,a L^2 = 1{,}464 \cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{m} ,\]

three quarters of the displacement of the lower end, as the dashed line at half the length in the displacement diagram shows. We got the same number to four digits in section 1.7.1 for the downward displacement of the point \(P\) at this depth (the difference is \(9{,}4 \cdot 10^{-13}\) m, because \(P\) is not on the axis).

Why three quarters? Figure 3.44 shows it. On the right is the bar before loading with marks at the top, at half the length and at the bottom, and beside it the same bar after loading with the same marks. The point \(O\) at the top is fixed, so the top mark has stayed in place. After loading the upper half is \(L/2\) long plus \(u(L/2) - u(0) = \tfrac34\,a L^2\), as far as the middle mark has moved. The lower half gets longer by \(u(L) - u(L/2) = \tfrac14\,a L^2\), three times less. The upper half is stretched more. On the left is the strain diagram of figure 3.43, split into the upper and the lower half. The average strain of the upper half is its elongation divided by its length, \(\tfrac34\,a L^2/(L/2) = 1{,}5\,aL\), that of the lower half \(\tfrac14\,a L^2/(L/2) = 0{,}5\,aL\). These are the strains (3.13) at the middles of the two halves, at the depth \(L/4\) and at the depth \(3L/4\), since \(2a\,(L - L/4) = 1{,}5\,aL\) and \(2a\,(L - 3L/4) = 0{,}5\,aL\). The strain falls evenly with depth, along a straight line, and the average of such a quantity over a half is just its value at the middle of the half. Hence the ratio \(1{,}5 : 0{,}5 = 3 : 1\).

The formula \(u(L) = \rho g L^2/(2E)\) also tells how the elongation depends on the material and on the thickness of the bar. Figure 3.45 shows four hanging bars \(10\) m long, each before loading and after it, with greatly exaggerated elongations. The elongation is proportional to \(\rho g/E\). Our steel bar gets longer by \(1{,}952 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m. A bar of a material twice as stiff, with the modulus \(2E\), gets longer by half as much, by \(0{,}976 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m, because \(E\) is in the denominator. A bar of a material twice as heavy, with the density \(2\rho\), gets longer by twice as much, by \(3{,}904 \cdot 10^{-5}\) m. A steel bar of diameter \(20\) mm gets longer by the same amount as ours. The thickness of the bar does not appear in the displacement, just as it did not appear in the stress (2.5). Twice the diameter gives four times the cross-sectional area, and each cross section carries four times the weight, so the stress at the top is \(765\,180\) Pa in both bars.

One more claim from chapter 1 is waiting to be confirmed. In section 1.2 we wrote that the hanging bar gets longer by the same amount as an equal bar whose weight is negligible and which is pulled at its lower end by a force equal to half the weight of the hanging bar (figure 1.25). The weight of the hanging bar is \(\rho g A L\). A bar pulled by the axial force \(N = \rho g A L/2\) gets longer by (3.2) by

\[\Delta L = \frac{N L}{E A} = \frac{\rho g A L \cdot L}{2 E A} = \frac{\rho g L^2}{2E} ,\]

which is exactly \(u(L)\), the elongation of the hanging bar.

In the displacement field (1.19), too, we now recognize both numbers of the material. Where \(a\) stood, there stands \(\rho g/(2E)\), where \(0{,}3\) stood, there stands \(\nu\), and \(0{,}6\,a = 2\nu\,\rho g/(2E) = \nu\,\rho g/E\):

\[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{x}} &= \frac{\rho g}{2E}\,(2Lx - x^2) - \frac{\nu\,\rho g}{2E}\,(y^2 + z^2) , \\ u_{\mathrm{y}} &= -\frac{\nu\,\rho g}{E}\,(L - x)\,y , \\ u_{\mathrm{z}} &= -\frac{\nu\,\rho g}{E}\,(L - x)\,z . \end{aligned}\]

This is how CM (7.3.20) (PDF p. 306) and SADD (5.7.4) (PDF p. 115) write the field, in axes placed differently. The component \(u_{\mathrm{y}}\) is \(-\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(x)\,y\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}(x)\) is the strain (3.13). So a point at the distance \(y\) from the axis moves towards the axis by \(\nu\) times the strain along the bar, multiplied by \(y\), and the lateral strain is \(\partial u_{\mathrm{y}}/\partial y = -\nu\,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{xx}}\), exactly as in a specimen by definition 3.8. Whether the field agrees with the relation between stress and strain in all other components too, we will check in section 3.2, when we write this relation in space.

The tension test gave us two numbers, \(E\) and \(\nu\). The first tells by how much a bar gets longer at a given stress, the second by how much it gets thinner at the same time. With them we computed in two steps the displacement of the hanging bar, which in chapter 1 was left without a derivation. The stress divided by \(E\) gave the strain at each point, and the displacement was the only function that has this strain as its derivative and is zero at the top. In a body, however, stresses act on the material in several directions at once, shear stresses too. How the material deforms then is the question of the next section.
